utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good morning to everyone. I have a few practical matters. First of all, the insurmountable problems turned out not to be insurmountable. That means that the week we're not sitting in October will be the week starting on Monday, the 11th, as I already indicated as the most likely solution. Then the second issue is how to proceed with the intercepts in relation to this witness. I think the Chamber sent a message yesterday that we intend to treat the comments as something that should not be put in front of the witness and just to be read or just to be confirmed, because it would come close to 92 bis or 89(F), and therefore, that's something that should be presented viva voce. One of the problems may be how to draw the attention on the relevant part of the transcript. Let's just see how it works, but perhaps a reference even to his comment, if it's not very much a contentious issue, could perhaps assist the witness, because otherwise he might have great difficulties in finding at all the spot and the context in which the questions are put to him. But as such, the comment whether something is very important or whether something is contradicting other parts is something we'd like to hear from the witness and not as a result of confronting the witness with what he stated earlier in these comments. Having said this, is there any further observation?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We're ready to proceed, Your Honour. I have asked a member of my staff to join us. He's a technical wizard, if you will, and I have asked him to sit in the rear. He'll come in, and in the event we have a development like we had yesterday, he should be able to assist us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, how nice for the Prosecution they're able to lay their hands on a technical wizard, because we have to double up with that task. Your Honour, we endorse, as Your Honour I think already knows informally, we endorse, with respect, what the Trial Chamber said about the handling of intercepts, which is completely in line with what we submitted yesterday. May we simply comment, certainly as far as directing a witness to the relevant part of the intercepts are concerned, that seems to be part of the normal challenge for an advocate to steer the examination efficiently. Your Honour, it would follow, we suggest, that the schedule containing the witness comments ought, as a matter of good practice, it ought to be retrieved from the Trial Chamber, because since that material is not going to be in evidence, that schedule in that form should be handed back by the Trial Chamber now, or -- well, not now. It doesn't have to be done this second, but at some convenient point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We might keep it for practical reasons at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Right now, of course, Your Honour. I'm sorry, I withdraw "now." That's absolutely not necessary, but at some suitable point because it isn't in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I simply comment, the report on the video, I delivered three videotapes with my own fair hands to the United Nations Detention Unit yesterday evening just before 8.00. I'm very --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I saw them leaving at 7.40.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I understood that Your Honour had seen them in one set of even fairer hands before they were handed to me. The -- Ms. Dixon, namely. Your Honour, they were, I'm happy to say, they were transmitted very quickly to Mr. Krajisnik, for which I'm grateful to all concerned at the UNDU. That doesn't, as a matter of fact, give him an enormous amount of time then at already 8.00 in the evening. It leads on to one simple practical matter that I've been meaning to mention for a couple of days, Your Honour, which is this: A long time ago, Your Honour invited the parties' views on preferences for sitting in the morning and the afternoon. I understand the Trial Chamber's preference is for mornings. As it happens, my own personal preference is for mornings, not entirely shared enthusiastically by every member of my team as a preference, but we all have our personal preferences. But there is a practical matter, Your Honour, which we are finding increasingly, which is that it is far more difficult to get useful time with Mr. Krajisnik when we sit in the morning, because the earliest we're really able to get to the Detention Unit then, and Mr. Krajisnik is able to get there, is around 3.00. We end up having about -- if Mr. Harmon could just let me finish on this, I think it would be useful. The -- we end up having a maximum of about an hour and a half after several hours in court. That is nowhere near as productive -- maybe Mr. Harmon is going to agree, Your Honour, but if I could just explain -- so I apologise if Mr. Harmon is about to signify agreement, but all the same, I would just like to indicate --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt, but there is a limited amount of time with this witness and this is a matter that seems could be taken up after court or at another time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It will take almost less than time than the comment, Your Honour. The morning will give us a clear run through. The practical suggestion I was going to make, Your Honour, was reserving our position on the overall schedule, but if we are sitting continuously, we wonder if it would be possible to alternate weeks of mornings and weeks of afternoons as a compromise. That's all I have to say on that subject, Your Honour. I'm sorry for Mr. Harmon's anxiety that his witness should get back to Sarajevo, which, of course, is understood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll consider that, and I do agree with Mr. Harmon that this is a matter, especially since it seems not to meet a lot of opposition, that could have been dealt with during a break and through the intermediary of one of our legal officers. But we certainly will consider it and it sounds fair what you say. Then could you, Madam Usher, escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning. Please sit down, Mr. Kljuic. May I remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony. Your examination will now continue. Mr. Harmon, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Harmon: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Kljuic. I would like to focus your attention to events that occurred in Bijeljina at the end of March and the beginning of April 1992. Bijeljina is a municipality in Bosnia that sits along the Drina River and is contiguous with Serbia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Da.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And from an ethnic composition point of view, the Muslims formed a minority in that particular municipality; correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Da.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges what happened to the Bosniak community in Bijeljina at the end of March 1992 and the beginning of April 1992.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, excuse me just a second. I may ask you to start again because we're not getting the English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: On channel 4 where I usually --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you hear the English?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now we can, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you, then, Mr. Kljuic, will you start again.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I was saying, before the incident in Bijeljina, there were a number of similar situations in the area of Bosnia-Herzegovina where we had the killing of people. However, the incident in Bijeljina had a very specific message to convey, and it was this: In addition to the Yugoslav army, there were paramilitary units that found themselves there of Serbs from Yugoslavia, and they were led by Zeljko Raznjatovic, better known as Arkan. He had his own units. In the Presidency, we received a report according to which it was said to be a question of conflicts; however, there was no fighting of partners that was taking place. What happened was that the Serb paramilitaries had started killing the Muslims and abusing them. Then we set up a state delegation --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you for just a moment, please, Mr. Kljuic. If I could have some exhibits shown to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: They would be two photographs. They're related photographs. If I could have a number on those.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit number P294A for ERN ending 098808, and P294B for ERN ending 098812.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Kljuic, are you familiar with these photographs?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court what these photographs depict?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On one of the photographs, you can see the victims and the brutality of this particular soldier who is hitting them. On the other photograph, probably the bereaved family of this first victim. However, I should like to say that these photographs are not secret photographs. They were in fact published, made public, after all this took place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, could you tell the Court --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Actually, Your Honours, let me just draw your attention to these two exhibits. You will notice that the woman who is on the ground in Prosecution Exhibit 294A is the same woman who is standing over the man who is laying on the ground. She is depicted in Exhibit 294B. So these are related photographs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Kljuic, if you could then tell us again what happened to the Muslim population and what the reaction was in the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is clear that the Muslim population, as a whole, was being intimidated and was afraid, and many of them were killed. A number of victims was never established. But when the Presidency delegation returned, and it comprised of members of the Presidency, Fikret Abdic, Biljana Plavsic, and the defence minister of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Jerko Doko, the reports coming in were contradictory, in fact. Fikret Abdic and Biljana Plavsic said that it was an incident which could be overcome, whereas my minister said that what he saw in Bijeljina was horrendous and that he, as the defence minister of Bosnia-Herzegovina, had to lie down on the ground and be disarmed when Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, gave the command, the order for him to do so. Now, that reports of this kind were quite normal and usual is borne out by a photograph when Biljana Plavsic, as member of the Presidency, embraced Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan. In that report, the one that came in, we see a polarisation of Bosnia-Herzegovina into two sides, those fighting against crimes and those supporting crimes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let me show you the next exhibit, Mr. Kljuic. You said that Mrs. Plavsic had formed part of the commission. Let me show you a film and then I'm going to ask you to comment on it. While we're waiting for this film to come up, until it does, what was the role of Mrs. Plavsic supposed to be in respect of her visit to Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, she was supposed to submit a realistic report, all the more so since she was the president of a commission within the Presidency in charge of the constitutional order. So this was the most responsible role in defending the constitutional order and system of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was she supposed to be a neutral and fair observer to the events in Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: She would have had to have been a just observer. But of course you can't be neutral, because the question is: What did Zeljko Raznjatovic's units do as paramilitary formations in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let me show, and you can see in front of you a monitor, you can see a film. It's very brief. I want to ask you your comments after you see this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I instruct the interpreters to read the English translation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] Momcilo Krajisnik showed our reporter today --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While we're trying to find this film, we will continue with the examination and I will be informed when this film is available on this system. What did Mrs. Plavsic report back to the Presidency as to what happened in Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, roughly speaking, she said there had been an incident, that the number of dead was not known, that it wasn't organised, that it was spontaneous, that it was a group of irresponsible young men who committed the act, and that the Muslims had probably caused the incident and that the killing was the result of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me show you -- now we have the film on. Let me show you the film and then I'm going to ask you for your comments, Mr. Kljuic. It should be on the monitor in front of you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] On behalf of the leadership of the SDS, Mrs. Plavsic, former member of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, publicly, in front of the eyes of the world, paid recognition to the Serbian --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's the end of the film. It's a very brief clip, Mr. Kljuic. Can you tell us what that film depicts?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can see a very warm relationship between Mrs. Plavsic and the leadership, or rather, the leader and organiser of the perpetrators of the crime. Instead of acting like a Presidency member of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is to say, the supreme state body, and protecting the interests of all citizens equally, without exception, regardless of their ethnicity and religion, Mrs. Plavsic kissed Arkan, which was a shocking thing to behold for all the people who were there, especially for the mothers, because even before that happened, Arkan had presented the image of a war criminal for everything that he did -- had done in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that gesture symbolic in the eyes of the non-Serbs in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain your answer, please.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is how it was: Because of Milosevic's policy and the overall plan that was being put into practice, there was less and less trust and confidence in Belgrade as the centre of the country and its institutions, and the least trust or greatest lack of confidence was expressed towards the army, which just had the name in nominal terms the Yugoslav People's Army, whereas judging by its leading cadres and the structure of the army itself, it was first and foremost a Serb army and a Montenegrin army. However, that was not its greatest handicap. The greatest handicap was that the people had lost their confidence in an army of that kind, and because before that time, in Croatia, it had shot at the people. The greatest way in which the army had compromised itself was subordination with the paramilitary formations. So that the ordinary citizen was easily able to conclude and deduce that the Yugoslav People's Army and the paramilitary formations and Biljana Plavsic, as one of the leaders of the Serbian Democratic Party, were all on the same side. Their conduct and behaviour gave rise to fear amongst the non-Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Kljuic, was Mr. Krajisnik aware of what happened in Bijeljina in March and April of 1992?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And would it be fair to say that Bijeljina represented the first municipality where ethnic cleansing of the Bosniaks took place?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Before Bijeljina, this was done in a Croatian village, in the one-time municipality of Ravno, in Eastern Herzegovina, in which the units of the Yugoslav People's Army and the Montenegrin reservists slaughtered the population. The reason given was that the village had armed itself and that there was Croatian terrorists there. However, neither on that occasion, nor previously in the events in Croatia, was there a single functionary of the SDS who did something about those crimes. And that is what happened in Bijeljina with the killings that took place there too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. That is an event that related to the Bosnian Croats. My question was: Is it fair to say that Bijeljina represented the first municipality where ethnic cleansing of the Bosniaks took place?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Da.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So before that incident, there was an event that was directed by the army against a certain village involving Bosnian Croats. That's what your testimony is; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Da.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, when the commission from the Presidency went to Bijeljina, was that as part of the Commission on Constitutional Order? Did they go in that capacity?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Da.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you tell the Court, first of all, were you a member of the Commission on Constitutional Order?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I did not get the English translation of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you repeat your answer, Mr. Kljuic. I'm sorry. I did not get the translation in English.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was. Mrs. Plavsic was the chairman and I was a member of that commission.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the Commission on Constitutional Order receive reports about events, violent events that were occurring in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In keeping with the method of work of the commission, it was supposed to receive all police records regarding all incidents happening at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Krajisnik receive copies of those reports, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Krajisnik, as speaker of the parliament, and Mr. Jure Pelivan, as Prime Minister, were receiving these reports.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that based on the reports that you were receiving in the commission and the reports that Mr. Krajisnik was receiving as well, that Mr. Krajisnik was informed about the situation on the ground in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think he was much better informed than the rest of us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if I could show you the next exhibit. It will be an exhibit that is P47. We have seen these exhibits before perhaps. P47 is a decision of the Bosnian Serb Assembly. It is dated the 12th of May, 1992, and it is signed by Momcilo Krajisnik, as the president of the national Assembly. In this particular exhibit, Mr. Kljuic, in the first paragraph, it says: "The strategic objectives or priorities of the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina are two: One, establish state borders separating the Serbian people from other two ethnic communities," and it has five additional objectives. In the Assembly, when this objectives were passed, Mr. Krajisnik, said the following. Let me quote this to you. This is found in Exhibit 65, binder 12, tabs 127 and 129. Mr. Krajisnik said to the assembled members of the Bosnian Serb Assembly: "As for the strategic goals, I would like to offer an explanation, since I have taken part in adopting these goals. We must make a choice regarding one thing. The first goal is the most important one, and in relation to all other goals, all other goals are sub-items to the first one." Now, I'd like you, Mr. Kljuic, to focus on the strategic objectives, the exhibits before you, and particularly, strategic objective number 1. And I'd like you to relate the events that took place in Bosnia before May the 12th to the SDS policy, and specifically to strategic objective number 1.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is abundantly clear that this decision is a component of Belgrade's global policy, because the leadership of Bosnia and Herzegovina's SDS was entrusted with the implementation of one aspect of that project that related to Bosnia and Herzegovina. We can see that this is true from para 4 of this decision, very clearly. In this paragraph, borders are explicitly established on the Una and Neretva River. Those are the maximised claims of Mr. Milosevic, geared at creating Greater Serbia. This 12th May decision, for purely practical reasons, in order to show people involved in armed combat that what they are doing is permitted and approved by this document, should dispel any doubt among the people wielding rifles. Namely, the very idea of separation is unnatural in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Communities could by no means be separated without brutal force, because the population was so intertwined, so mixed, that even on the level of individual families, people belonged to different ethnic groups. On the other hand, the idea about forcible separation of communities implies the breakup of Bosnia and Herzegovina. At the time when this was published, the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina had already been internationally recognised. Ten days after this decision, we were to become a member of the United Nations, at the same time as Slovenia and Croatia. And finally, these decisions very eloquently speak to the fact that they were aware they had to achieve their aims by violence. We only have to see para 2, which reads that the corridor from Western Bosnia to Semberija had to be protected. Because this corridor passes through majority Croat and majority Muslim populated centres, this corridor was not easy to ensure. For some people, this may have come as a surprise, but for those who had been closely following the developments in Bosnia and Herzegovina, this document, with this wording, in this shape, was known as part of Mr. Milosevic's global plan for the creation of Greater Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Kljuic, were these objectives that you have before you that were promulgated on the 12th of May, were these an epiphany for the Bosnian Serb leadership or were these essentially an expression of policy that the Bosnian Serbs, including Mr. Krajisnik, had expressed to you earlier and had been following?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is genuinely the political platform of the SDS, with the proviso that it is systematised in this document and presented in a sequence that reflects priorities. It had never before been presented this way. But the everyday conduct of the SDS and the things that they always insisted on are reflected here in this programme. In their entire political conduct over the several months after the elections, prior to the aggression, their political conduct and their conduct on the ground, that is, violence, was contrary to the content of these decisions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after the promulgation of these strategic objectives, how did events play out on the ground in respect of the separation and the division of non-Serb ethnic communities?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After 2nd May, which is considered to be the date of the beginning of the aggression, military operations of Bosnian Serbs, synchronised with the actions of the JNA, paramilitary units, as well as the local armed population, were horrific. First of all, at that time, people were confused. They were not expecting their neighbours to drive them out of their homes. It is the time when the greatest crimes were committed, because in a military onslaught, for which they had been well prepared, Bosnian Serbs captured a large chunk of territory. There is evidence that as far back as June 1992, they held, for all practical purposes, about 70 per cent of BH territory. In order to attain this goal, many crimes were committed. And it was a fortunate non-Serb who was allowed to be deported. I must recall here that many had to pay for this freedom, and all of them had to sign away their assets. Such a blitzkrieg against an unprepared and unarmed population, many among whom had never thought that things would end that way, seemed to have encouraged Karadzic and the SDS leadership to continue with their ultimatums. This policy, sponsored by Slobodan Milosevic, would become dominant first of all in the summer of 1992 with the London peace conference and onwards throughout their negotiations, mediated first by Vance and Owen and later by Owen and Stoltenberg, in Geneva and other places. What horrified the entire world, including ourselves who could not possibly expect this, is the intensity and the way these crimes were being committed. Hundreds of people were forced to flee. Many were killed at their doorstep. And due to the military superiority they had, with regard to large cities, especially Sarajevo, where I spent four years of the war, they used daily shelling and sniping.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, the question was a very general one. It's just disappearing off the screen, but how did events play out on the ground in respect of the division? It is so general that it is tantamount to inviting the witness, "Give us an account of what happened in former Yugoslavia, in Bosnia and Herzegovina, at this time." It's not exactly that. That's a slight exaggeration. But it is that order of question. That, therefore, raises a serious question as to how far this witness ought to be giving evidence of these matters. And by analogy with what we considered yesterday, where the question arose of laying of the proper factual basis and the Trial Chamber indicated that it was permitting Mr. Harmon considerable flexibility as to whether he asked a general question first and then explored the factual foundation or did it the other way around, there nevertheless does have to be that. In relation to this particular witness, Your Honour, we're getting into an area where it is extremely important, first of all, that the witness's evidence is confined -- well, first of all, to what he knows. Secondly, Your Honour, that it's confined so as to exclude material where there are other witnesses who either already have done or will do or far more appropriately might cover some of this ground. But at the very least, these general questions, which then lead to general answers, must be supplemented, we submit, by specific questions which enable everybody, and particularly the Trial Chamber, of course, to see precisely where it is this witness gets this information from and precisely the limits of his knowledge and what the sources are.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm more than happy to respond. In the description of Mr. Kljuic's qualifications, he testified that he was a -- Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond between April of 1992 and October of 1993, the president of the State Commission for Gathering Information on War Crimes, and he remained in that commission and a member of that body until the end of 1993. I think Mr. Kljuic is well informed about the crimes that took place on the ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me ask Mr. Kljuic. Would you please indicate clearly when giving this rather wide answer, broad answers, whether you gained that knowledge in your capacity as a member of that committee or whether your sources were otherwise. What you just told us until now, what was the source?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My sources are primarily my own empirical knowledge; second, the political information that was available to me as member of the state leadership; and third, information available to the commission in charge of gathering evidence of war crimes, which I first led and in which I later continued to work as a member, and which followed the Wiesenthal method. I stayed in that commission until 1994. The commission gathered information from the victims. At the time, this was a commission of great import, in which I was only the chairman. But the real authors who worked on the collection of evidence were lawyers, young international law experts, and every day we had ample opportunity to watch all sorts of TV channels and listen to the radio, and I can tell you that the greatest amount of information was available from the radio and television of Bosnian Serbs who never made any effort to conceal what was happening on the ground. I believe, by the way, that everybody who wanted to get informed anywhere in the world had enough information available from Bosnia and Herzegovina to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, on the basis of the variety of sources the witness uses, and also the -- well, possible difference in quality of these kind of sources, because media sources are quite different from what you learn in your capacity as a member of a committee who receives reports on what happened on the ground, would you please try to get as detailed information every time what the source of the witness's knowledge is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes. I'd be glad to, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, could we also say that yes, although it is quite true that Mr. Kljuic's position as the president of this particular commission is mentioned as effectively part of his curriculum vitae, that is a very different matter from him coming here and now apparently seeking to give fairly extensive evidence - because that's one of the categories, it's one of the sources - derived from and based upon that position. That really is a step well beyond what could reasonably be gathered from that being included as one of his bits of experience. It's a large and significant area, and we submit that it's not appropriate for his evidence now to go into that realm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I gave guidance to Mr. Harmon. Please proceed, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, would it be fair to say that the events in Bijeljina were a preview of things to come during the war?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. That was a message that all those who would not obey and accept the political ultimatums of the SDS would end up the same way as the Muslims in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I would like to play for you a film clip.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This is a film clip, Your Honour, of the 34th session of the Bosnian Serb Assembly. The date of this is the 27th of August, 1993. We have a transcript. A transcript has been provided to the booth, and as soon as the transcript is disseminated, we will play this particular clip.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then, Mr. Kljuic, after this clip is played, I would like to ask you some questions about a particular part of this clip. All right. I think we can now proceed with the video.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I see lips moving on the video, and this is a bad sign, because I don't hear any sound coming.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Neither do I, Mr. Harmon, but since you've got your wizard with you ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps we can start this again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, as you know, I'm not a wizard, but if you have copied these video clips on CD-ROMs, rather than start searching through all of the hard disks somewhere, rather play it from the CD-ROM, which is, I think, a very practical solution.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour -- sorry. We are in the middle of a task. While all this is happening, Your Honour, what -- by supplementing a submission I made a few minutes ago. What I would wish to do would be to draw the Court's attention very specifically to the 65 ter summary provided in relation to this witness, because -- and it may be that Your Honours would wish to see that specifically. Because those 65 ter summaries do have a purpose, and the evidence which we have been hearing over the last 10 or 15 minutes is, in our submission, going far beyond the scope of the 65 ter summary, and after all, we note the purpose is essentially to give an indication, in fairly broad terms, but to give an indication of the areas and the topics that are to be covered. Nobody objects to sensible flexibility at the margins involving a margin of appreciation, and from time to time, of course, it's quite natural that additional areas are indicated between the sometimes long-ago service of the 65 ter and the actual evidence. But that's a different matter. What we have here is information or evidence which goes way beyond that. Your Honour, is it helpful for Your Honour to -- I've only got -- there seem to be two versions. They may be very slightly different. I can't explain that immediately. I think what happens is they're often updated and a new one is served. I think there was one in 2001 and another one in 2002. Would it be helpful for the Trial Chamber to have an opportunity at some convenient point of seeing these summaries?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber would like to have them available during the next break so we can --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. During the next break, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: During the next break.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm obliged. Yes. We'll organise that as soon as we can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I apologise for this. Could we have a break for a few minutes and we will try to resolve this as quickly as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll -- the Chamber will remain --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm told it has arrived. Let's see if we have some sound on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's see whether it now works.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let's take a break, Your Honour. I think that ... Your Honour, I think it would be appropriate to take a break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. What we could do is to have our early break now. We would then restart at 10.30. Then continue -- well, I'll think about the schedule to follow, but let's have a break for 25 minutes, and please find all wizards in the building, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, I do understand that the technical problems have not been solved and that you will proceed by other means. That's point one. Second point: The Chamber has considered during the break the 65 ter summary, which is a very broad summary, which covers a large area, and taking into account the time when the 65 ter summary was delivered, and also taking into account later statements provided to the Defence, the Chamber does not consider it inappropriate to deal with the matters as you have done until now. So please proceed, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, do I have the opportunity of making submissions on that matter? Because I simply have handed up the 65 ter summary with a view to Your Honours reading it, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You also added a few words to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: In advance, Your Honour, yes, but then I stopped because I realised that there was not much value in my going into it in any detail before Your Honours had seen the piece of paper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, from what I remember - but let's just check it - you told us that on the basis of the 65 ter summary, it was inappropriate to deal with the matters --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. I did, Your Honour. That was my basic submission. But what I didn't do then was point Your Honours to specific aspects of the 65 ter summary when Your Honours were at the disadvantage of not having seen it. I've stated what my point is but in order to make it good I would like the opportunity of referring to the summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber has based its decision on your basic observations in this respect. The Chamber has read the 65 ter summary. If there's anything to be added, you're free to do so, but please, in writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, how can I do it in writing, with respect, in time for the point to be taken on board? The witness is giving his evidence. If I give it -- if I now -- even if I were to leave Court, which is not really a fair thing to expect me to do, how can I do that, Your Honour, with respect, in time for the matter to be properly dealt with? This witness is giving evidence on these matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll just check what you said at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, with respect, checking what I said, my submissions -- as I'd indicated, Your Honour, my submissions were not made at that point and not intended to be made, because in fairness to the Trial Chamber and everybody, I wished to give the Trial Chamber the opportunity of looking at the 65 ter summary before I made specific submissions on the matter. Your Honour is coming dangerously close to shutting the Defence out from making proper submissions on an important matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You agree that you mainly have drawn our attention to the 65 ter, although you clearly indicated what the purpose of the 65 ter summary was and that it went far beyond that. You have two minutes to make any submissions if you want to do it orally at this moment, Mr. Stewart. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. The particular point in the 65 ter submission, given that I've only got two minutes, relates to the work of this commission. The witness does not indicate -- the 65 ter summary does not indicate that the scope of the witness's evidence is going to include the details of the work of the commission looking into war crimes and any information obtained by him in relation to that matter. Neither does the statement -- there is not a section of that statement, there is not an area of that statement relating to this matter at all. We, in fairness, could have been given and have been given no indication whatever that the area of what actually happened during the war, as opposed to before, and the areas that the witness went into based, it seems at least partly, on information that he had gathered through his work on that war crimes investigative commission, there's not the slightest indication, in fairness, that we would have faced that particular area, and that was the ambit of -- included within the ambit of this witness's evidence. That, Your Honour, is the essential point here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The witness described in general terms what happened in Bosnia and Herzegovina. We have been in trial submitting evidence through the various crime-base witnesses precisely addressing that fact. Mr. Kljuic gave some general and summary observations about what happened. He added no additional details than what we've had probably 30 or 40 witnesses describing with painful and detailed particularity.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, if he's going to stop there and he's going no further into this area in the course of his evidence, then we don't need to consider this matter any more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, any --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: He's not going to go additionally farther than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then the matter seems to be resolved. Madam Usher, could you please escort the witness into the courtroom. You may proceed, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, my apologies for the technical problems that we've been experiencing. I was going to play for you a video clip of the portion of the 34th session of the Bosnian Serb Assembly. Instead I have a transcript of that. I'm unable to resurrect the actual video. So I will read this to you, and then I will ask you some questions about it. I will begin my reading: "MOMCILO KRAJISNIK: Mr. Rajko Kasagic. Mr. Dragan Micic will follow. "RAJKO KASAGIC: Ladies and gentlemen, at this difficult moment it is difficult to be wise. One should be prescient to be able to say what will be achieved. Nevertheless, this Assembly constantly adopted, with the utmost seriousness, certain decisions, especially these. And therefore, in my assessment it is irresponsible whoever says ..." and there's a break. "I am an attorney, a certain percentage of the decisions is implemented through the courts, and a percentage is not. Whether decisions will be implemented depends on the strength of the state. When the state, a state ensuring the rule of law is stronger, then they must all be implemented. This is a game played by the international community and the world against the Serbian people. In the division of the world, as they say, in the new international order, there are maps where there are no Serbs in these parts. We see yet another trap for the Serbs, constructed in the bamboozling period of Broz, as Mr. Krajis ... Karadzic said, in 'Broz's boozling' period. They recognised the Muslim nation and we thought, that's what they told us, that this was democracy. But this recognition was not free --" there's a question mark, it may be in vain. "We even hear that even the Islamic world received a lot of money. And why? Because of their own state, because each people has a right to its state. They are not interested in just this small enclave depicted on our territory in the former Bosnia-Herzegovina. Take a look at these pockets around the Drina River and that part of Posavina. These are pockets where they who support the dispersal of the Serbs and ... the establishment of an Islamic world in these parts, their state, are always ready to jump into the fray against us, against the Serbian people. And why? Their oil is cheap. It costs 55 cents a barrel because of the boreholes which are cheap, in comparison with 18 dollars in other areas. They are not interested in the Serbian people or in friendship, the centuries-old friendship that someone invokes, not even in trade relations. They are interested in today's situation, in today's oil. I would therefore broach the matter with seriousness for us to separate for all time, although I assert there will be no peace in these parts. This assessment is shared by some of my friends who are in the military. They know a lot more about that. Look at who is paying for this --" and then there's an unintelligible word and the sentence continues -- "the Serbs in Sarajevo and the Serbs in Krajina, I would accept a Bosnian Krajina, but I refer to it as Banja Luka Krajina, to differentiate it from the Republic of the Serbian Krajina. We are closed off. It is what we fought against. We fought for the state of Krajina, unity ... a unified state of all Serbs in the areas of the former Bosnia and Herzegovina. We are now getting what we fought against. We are closed off at Brcko and I think that we cannot accept these maps with that. At the very least, the borders must be --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, yes. Mr. Harmon, I noticed that the French translation was approximately eight lines behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. I'll slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I mean, by the end, we have to wait anyhow until they're finished. So please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: "At the very least the borders must be where they are at present, at Vrba. They cannot be moved an inch towards Brcko because all sorts of infrastructure must make its way through these parts. If we already know that we must be ready for war, against that enemy which has expansions for the world, how should we arm ourselves? It is easy to bring weapons through Romania and even Hungary. We did not wage war against them, but we are waging war with these people here. How are we to arm ourselves via Brcko? And especially this demilitarisation, as they refer to it, I think it was precisely prepared so America, which prepared it in Broz's time, together with the Arabic world to give them a state. No one would give up war if this part of Brcko were to be given. And according to that agreement, as they refer to it, Annex A, Part 2, if one republic should leave Bosnia and Herzegovina, the federation ..." then there's a break -- "it remains in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Well, I concluded it was Sarajevo, although I did not clearly see what Annex A, Part 2 meant. If we have to yield that, and our second dream, the next stage is separation and linking up with the Serbian states, to separate completely and have no joint organs with those against whom we are at war today. Let us then give that Sarajevo of ours and make them pay as much as it is worth. I am not a patriot, a local patriot, but I am thinking of achieving our unity, not to mention our wealth in some future time, although there may be a big question mark there. That's what I wanted to say. Thank you. "MOMCILO KRAJISNIK: I have to intervene. This is another discussion which is not appropriate now. And I think that Mr. Kasagic, in addition to Mr. Micic, is speaking of something that really is not appropriate. First, there are 150.000 Serbs in Sarajevo. Second, there are resources which we have to preserve. Third, the people have safeguarded that and if they have accepted it as a temporary solution, I do not think that it is appropriate to make proposals now. Although Rajko is my good friend, I want to ask him not to make such proposals, especially since we have agreed to preserve that part of the Serb Sarajevo where a large number of people were killed but it was not greatly publicised, and now all these deputies are silent because they think that someone else will solve that on their behalf. If you want me to say so, gentlemen, the Muslims ... the Croats sought ... and the Muslims sought a municipality in Banja Luka. And we did not accept it, because that territory of ours must be clean. And I wish to ask you not to trade territories when you really are not abreast of things. I must react, although it is not appropriate that I react from here as the president of the Assembly. I thought what Mr. Micic said was a joke. But now there is a gradual and serious discussion about giving 150.000 Serbs for at least 15 cities which have 15.000 residents. And I wish to ask you to get serious and make serious proposals, although we do not have such ... I am not accustomed to speak in this tone. Go ahead ... "MALE VOICE: I just want to ask ... What is Annex 2, Part 2? "MOMCILO KRAJISNIK: I don't know. You can find it in the copy. "MALE VOICE: I think it is Sarajevo ... We are offering it for free ... "MOMCILO KRAJISNIK: We are not offering it for free. Instead, there will be a provisional solution for two years, and everyone stays in their areas. "MALE VOICE: ... then it will never be settled ... "MOMCILO KRAJISNIK: And please don't ..." Then there's an unintelligible male voice and then: "MOMCILO KRAJISNIK: Please, if you are interested, if you are interested in Sarajevo, there are deputies here ... for a period of two years, Sarajevo is a provisional solution, and everyone remains in their ethnic areas. It is really not appropriate to discuss whether the Serbs will hold on to it or not, if we yield that area, look at how big that area is over here. And if we start to argue now, we will accomplish nothing. Go ahead ... Addresses Micic, who is waiting to speak. "DRAGAN MICIC: Mr. President, fellow deputies ..." And that concludes then my reading of this portion of the transcript from the 34th Assembly session, Bosnian Serb Assembly session of the 22nd of August, 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Kljuic, let me direct your attention to a portion of the comments that were made by Mr. Krajisnik, and then I would like to get your reaction to them in relation to what these comments relate to and how they relate to the strategic objectives. So let me read this portion again. This is Mr. Krajisnik. "MOMCILO KRAJISNIK: If you want me to say so, gentlemen, the Muslims, the Croats sought, and the Muslims sought a municipality in Banja Luka and we did not accept it because that territory of ours must be clean." Can you please comment on that statement by Mr. Krajisnik made in 1993 and related it to the strategic objectives, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I notice that the French interpreters are ready now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you for that intervention, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, did you understand my question? And if you did, could you please give us your answer.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This Assembly, the Serb Assembly, which was held in the summer of 1993, while the peace negotiations were going on in Geneva, it was held at the same time. The Geneva negotiations had several stages, several maps speaking about Bosnia's division and proposals put forward. Now, at the Assembly, there are two things that clearly state that the Serb deputies were facing a dilemma. They were motivated by their belonging to people from the territory; those who were in Sarajevo and in the environs of Sarajevo would not allow Sarajevo to be exchanged for some other territory somewhere else. Whereas those who came from outside Sarajevo, they didn't have the same sentiments and feeling for Sarajevo, so they agreed to forfeit Sarajevo in order to gain other territories. Now, for me, the principle applied by Mr. Krajisnik seems to me to be all important here. I should like to remind you that in the city of Banja Luka, for example, there were 60.000 Croats and Muslims living there. So they were not able to gain a municipality, not because they were not deserved to have one, in view of their numbers, but they were not able to get a municipality because the Serbs wanted a pure territory. So this idea of ethnically pure territories was one of the causes and one of the reasons for the ethnic cleansing which was put into practice in all the areas in which the Serbs had taken control.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then how do you relate, Mr. Kljuic, that ethnically pure territories to strategic objective number 1 that was promulgated on the 12th of May?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The areas which they planned to attach, first of all, the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the discussions that were heard, you heard that the Serbian Krajina already existed on the territory of the Republic of Croatia, for instance. So in the final stages of realising the project of a Greater Serbia, all those territories were supposed to unite, to form one single Serbian state. And that was the objective of Milosevic's message before the war, that all Serbs had to live in one state. And those people delving in political history, they will know that 65 years ago there was another such man in Europe who said that the Germans had to live in the same state. And therefore, in a state of that kind, there could be no place for other ethnic groups. And in Banja Luka, there could be no place for the 60.000 Croats and Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Kljuic, can you inform this Trial Chamber what Mr. Krajisnik's position was post-Dayton in respect of the separation of ethnic groups.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, after Karadzic was eliminated, Karadzic who even hadn't been in Dayton, Mr. Karadzic was the first among Bosnian Serbs, and as such came onto the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina that had three members in 1995, 1996. The change was that it only had three members instead of the previous six. All of them had to respect the decisions of the Dayton Accords, and an essential annex of the Dayton Accords is annex number 7, which deals with the return of refugees to their homes. However, the Dayton Accords stipulated that Serbian forces in Bosnia had to leave certain territories that they had conquered and that, according to the accords, belonged to the Federation. Among those territories were some areas that had suffered from the most radical ethnic cleansing, including Sarajevo and some of its neighbourhoods, Grbavica, part of Hrasnica, Vogosca, Ilijas. Under the Dayton Accords, those areas were included in the Federation, and our Presidency sent an appeal to the Serbs, who had done no wrong and committed no crimes, calling upon them to feel free to stay in those territories because there was a general amnesty in place, and all their rights on the territory of the Federation were being guaranteed. However, a part of the Serbian leadership did not wish those people to remain in the territory of the Federation, despite the fact that many Serbs were locals there, especially in Ilijas, Vogosca, and Grbavica. The transition of territories towards the Federation was gradual, one or two municipalities each month. However, the leadership in Pale insisted that the Serbs who found themselves in places included in the Federation should leave their homes and move to Republika Srpska. That was a painful and very dramatic process in which people were burning their own homes and leaving into the unknown. There are many documents about this TV footage, interviews with those Serbs, who always ended up saying those were the orders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was Mr. Krajisnik's position in respect of whether the Serbs should remain within the territories that were non-Serbian?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To say the least, although he was a member of the Presidency, he didn't stop them or try to make them stay in the territory of the Federation. He didn't make a single public gesture inviting them to stay in their homes. Whether he personally issued orders that they should leave the areas that belonged to the Federation, I can't say, but it was evident that he was the highest Serb authority in Bosnia and Herzegovina. There are certain indications, but, Your Honours, I have no specific data.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me turn my attention to another subject, Mr. Kljuic, and that is, turn your attention to 1991 and 1992. Can you tell this Court what sources of information were available to you that were reporting ethnic cleansing that was occurring in Bosnia and Herzegovina? Just identify them.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A large number of policemen remained loyal to the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and in the course of performing their regular duties, these policemen reported on the situation on the ground. On the other hand, speaking of Croats, we had detailed reports from our citizens, reports from the ground, sent by fax and relating day-to-day events in certain territories, indicating the great losses we were suffering, primarily in terms of dismissals, requisition of material assets, but also Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond killings, rapes, and deportations into concentration camps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of international news media sources and other independent third-party sources of information was available to you about the ethnic cleansing that was occurring in Bosnia in 1991 and 1992? Can you just identify the sources, the media sources.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must tell you that the press was primarily represented by the British and American media. There was also the French minister, Bernard Kouchner, and they had the opportunity to visit territories held by Serbs, including Sarajevo. There was American journalist Burns, Christiane Amanpour, SkyNews television, and they were the only ones at the time, American reporters, who crossed the entire territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there other sources of information available to you, Mr. Kljuic, including the reports of Mr. Mazowiecki, Mr. Bassiouni, Bosnian news sources, Serbian news sources, NGOs, the United Nations, UNPROFOR, ICRC? Were they providing information about what was happening on the ground in Bosnia in 1991, 1992?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. A broad circle of people, whether they were Doctors Without Borders or Pharmacists Without Borders, or some other group, as well as inspectors and investigators of the United Nations, such as Cherif Bassiouni, and Mr. Mazowiecki and Mr. Bernard Kouchner, whom I mentioned earlier, was there. And we also had the reports of the UNPROFOR, who was a neutral force in Bosnia-Herzegovina, reporting like this, for instance: In the area of such-and-such town, shooting was heard, followed by transportation of some people to the hospital. However, if there was a person who knew the identity of these people, it always turned out that these were victims of Serb violence. As for Mr. Mazowiecki, there were direct instructions by the UN Security Council to conduct an inspection in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and these inspections provided the best confirmation of the actual situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina in those territories that were held by Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have three exhibits now. These are the Mazowiecki reports to the United Nations dated the 28th of August, 1992, followed by a report of the 27th of October, 1992, followed by a third report of the 17th of November, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While these documents are distributed, Mr. Harmon, I'd like to seek one clarification. You told us about American reporters being able to visit different areas. Was there -- were their reports also broadcast? So would you have access to their reports?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. These reports were published in American newspapers, and John Burns received the Pulitzer prize for his reporting from Bosnia-Herzegovina. I had an opportunity to see his articles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So they were published in American newspapers. Were the television programmes, the -- well, let's say the American television programme, were they aired in the region?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, John Burns was reporting for the New York Times. Second, we were able to watch SkyNews television and CNN. Christiane Amanpour, CNN reporter, came to Sarajevo several times in 1992, and among other things, she called on me at the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I just want to know whether in the area one could receive these programmes, and your answer to that is yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could I have the exhibit numbers for those three particular exhibits.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The 28th of August, 1992 report, P295. The 17th November, 1992 report, P296. And the 27 October 1992 report, P297.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could the witness be provided with copies of those reports. It should be copies in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, let me first of all ask you: Do you know who Mr. Mazowiecki is?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he was a former Prime Minister of Poland, was he not?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me read you from his reports two excerpts from his reports, and then I will seek your comments on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This first report that I'm quoting, Your Honour, is the report of the 27th of October, which is P297, and I direct your attention to paragraph 6 in that particular report, the report of October 27th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me quote from paragraph 6: "The Special Rapporteur shares the view of other observers that the principal objective of the military conflict in Bosnia and Herzegovina is the establishment of ethnically homogenous regions. Ethnic cleansing does not appear to be the consequence of the war, but rather its goal. This goal, to a large extent, has already been achieved through killings, beatings, rape, destruction of houses, and threats." Now, let me turn to another portion of Mr. Mazowiecki's report. This is the report of the 17th of November, 1992, Prosecutor Exhibit 296. And let me direct your attention and the Court's attention to paragraph 12, which is found in the section "Bosnia and Herzegovina ethnic cleansing general observations." I'm going to be reading you a portion of paragraph 12. Let me read from that portion: "The greater prevalence of ethnic cleansing in Serbian-occupied territories is undoubtedly related to the political objectives formulated and pursued by Serbian nationalists, namely, ensuring Serbian control over all territories inhabited by significant numbers of Serbs, as well as adjacent territories assimilated to them owing to logistical and military considerations. It should be noted that ethnic cleansing is not practiced exclusively in areas where Serbs form a majority of the population. In some of the cities most strongly affected by Serbian ethnic cleansing, such as Prijedor, Muslims and Croats were in the majority." Do you agree with the observations made by Mr. Mazowiecki?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you reviewed the reports of Mr. Mazowiecki and do you find them to be objective?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to have --

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- passed out.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, are we going to get -- may I ask, are we going to get the specific, factual foundation in terms of this witness's own knowledge and sources which enable him to make -- give such a sweeping answer which is in effect to introduce with an endorsement a very substantial report obtaining this witness's imprimatur once again clearly beyond the scope of the 65 ter and, on any fair reading, beyond the scope of the statement that's been offered to the Court as well. This really is, Your Honour, going, once again, too far.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, this basis of Mr. Kljuic's conclusions that there was ethnic cleansing was already described by Mr. Kljuic who was a member of the state commission. Two, he has discussed the political objectives at length. He was a participant for many years in these discussions with Mr. Krajisnik, Mr. Karadzic, Mrs. Plavsic, and Mr. Koljevic. He had intimate knowledge of what those objectives were and what the objectives that had been described by this report. So this -- that is the basis of the endorsement of Mr. Mazowiecki's independent conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I thought we were told expressly about 45 minutes ago that there was going to be no further evidence in this area from this witness. And here we are.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is a repeat of the evidence that we've heard for over a year in this case. This witness should be permitted to conclude his testimony. The fact that there was ethnic cleansing in Bosnia is not a surprise. It was something that has been the testimony and the subject of numerous witnesses who have testified.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So what's the position, Your Honour; any witness can come and give evidence about anything because we've heard some evidence from other witnesses about it? And over a year, it's only just a few weeks over a year that I came into this case at all, and it's about a year since Ms. Loukas came into this case at all. This is indiscipline of the way this trial is proceeding, Your Honour, because it is not, with respect, open to the Prosecution to just produce any witness to cover any ground that's been covered by anybody. We need to know and can fairly require to know in relation to any witness what are the areas he's going to cover. And specifically this morning that Mr. Harmon's comment then is no answer at all to my absolutely well-founded objection that we were told about 45 minutes ago, or 50 minutes ago now, that there would be no more evidence from this witness in this area, and there is now more evidence being adduced on this witness in this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, these reports -- Defence was informed that these were going to be exhibits in this trial. They were informed --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That doesn't answer the question, Your Honour. It doesn't answer my objection one bit. What about what was said 45 or 50 minutes ago and the fact that what is now happening is in direct contradiction of what we were expressly assured 50 minutes ago?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber has considered the matter and allows Mr. Harmon to proceed, especially in view of the last questions, whether the witness agreed with the conclusions of Mr. Mazowiecki. Of course the Chamber keeps in mind that the witness has testified that he received large portions of information from several sources, and Mr. Harmon is asking whether the conclusions reached by Mr. Mazowiecki, as he said, needed any comment or that the witness would agree. Of course, that does not mean that the Chamber accepts all the factual bases for such an assessment just on the basis of that report or on the basis of this testimony. The Chamber will consider this part of the testimony in connection with other factual evidence that is presented or will further be presented. Mr. Harmon --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I say that I wish to put on record that I specifically sat down and said no more on this matter about 50 minutes ago, trusting the assurance I was offered that there would be no more evidence in this area. And in future, the Defence will need to be considerably more wary of such assurances received from the Prosecution and through the Trial Chamber in relation to such matters if those assurances are going to be broken in this blatant way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The first is put on record. The second comment is also on record. Please proceed, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes. If I could have the next exhibit, Prosecution Exhibit 298, distributed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just ask you one thing. I think you dealt with two out of the three exhibits you presented; that is, the 17th of November and the -- no. First the 27th of October, 1992, and then the 17th of November, 1992. You also presented -- let me just have a look.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: There are three, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then the 28th of August. Although I'm a bit -- oh, I see that the 27th of October is again attached to the 28th of August document. Perhaps ... Yes, I see. We have a double now. In 295 we have two times -- we have also a reproduction of 297.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Apologies, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I mention, because it's a convenient point to mention, we were only notified yesterday, at about 20 past 1.00, after this witness had already been giving evidence for several hours, we were only notified yesterday that this particular batch of exhibits were to be used at all in relation to this witness. And that is not good enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, I do not fully remember. Were they on your list distributed earlier?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I will check, Your Honour. I am assuming they were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If they were, then of course the objection lacks --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's when we got the list, Your Honour. That's what I'm saying. The -- yesterday --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I do understand. I thought it was an earlier list at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, there was, and they weren't on it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber would like to know whether they were on the initial list or whether these exhibits were distributed --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I should be careful because I'm not even sure there was an earlier list. Ms. Cmeric is highly sceptical there was an earlier list, but if there was, then these items weren't on it, but we actually think there wasn't even a list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think as a matter of fact that I saw an earlier list, but I'm not quite sure about that. The Chamber would like to be informed whether for the first time these exhibits were announced to be used in relation to this witness only yesterday or that it was at an earlier stage, and the Chamber will consider that if the Defence would either need additional time for preparation of cross-examination or would express a wish to recall the witness for further cross-examination. Please proceed, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour. Thank you very much. Yes, Your Honour. Thank you very much. This is a copy -- the next exhibit is a copy of an article, of an interview with Mr. Krajisnik. It is from Glas Serbski in Banja Luka and it is dated the 8th of September, 1992. And I will read a portion of this interview. First reading the question and then reading Mr. Krajisnik's answer. Question: "Mr. President, mainly on the basis of the report of the former Polish Prime Minister, Tadeusz Mazowiecki, the UN Commission for Human Rights adopted a resolution by which Serbs are exclusively blamed for the genocide." Mr. Krajisnik's answer: "To be honest, I would not expect in my wildest dreams some former Prime Minister of a country to be so partial. Mazowiecki wrote his report in his office, as ordered, and not on the spot. Because if he were to write the report at the same time while he was visiting almost all camps and collection centres in the area of the former BH, then he would not accuse the Serbian people so easily as he did. Fortunately, Elie Wiesel, a Nobel prize winner, visited us and I believe that a man like him would be more honest and would never allow himself to be bribed. Mazowiecki wrote a report, was ordered by somebody, not an honest, credible report, on the breaking of human rights on the territory of the former BH."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Kljuic, very quickly and very succinctly, do you know by reputation Mr. Mazowiecki and whether he is such a man to have been bribed, to have not been honest and who would be partial in his examination of the events on the ground in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do know Mr. Mazowiecki. His findings, as far as we're concerned, were not a surprise but were important because they confirmed this and presented to the United Nations, which was -- which led up to the UN Resolution 725 or 727 - I'm not quite sure of the number - which was to be --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: This is not an answer --

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- voted on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: This is not an answer to the question, and moreover, the answer to the question, though in a sense the bare answer "I do know Mr. Mazowiecki" could in theory just leave it to cross-examination to explore what that means, given the range of possibilities as to what that means, we suggest that something more specific should be required, because, after all, all of us might know a particular or know of a particular figure, in which case, any particular person's evidence is of no value.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Have you ever met Mr. Mazowiecki?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course. I had three official meetings with Mr. Mazowiecki.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you with that answer. Is there -- do you have any reason or any fact available to you which would support a claim that Mr. Mazowiecki was bribed or ordered to write his report as he did?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it was like this: It would be possible to claim this only if you were the Serb side. The whole world knows that Mazowiecki was sincere. I don't know anybody who would be able to bribe Mazowiecki.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you say there's no fact known to you, neither is there any reason to believe that. The answer could have been a simple no. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me then conclude this. Based on the information that was available to you through the media sources, through reports like Mr. Mazowiecki -- it's a very simple question, but do you believe that Mr. Krajisnik was fully informed about the ethnic cleansing that was occurring in Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1992?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do believe that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to play an intercept, if I could. It's the next exhibit. This is an intercept from Exhibit 282, and I want to give --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, is Mr. Harmon going to explore the factual basis of the witness's assertion of belief that Mr. Krajisnik was fully informed about the ethnic cleansing? It's what one might regard as a relatively central issue in this case, and really a question for the Trial Chamber ultimately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Before I would intervene, I was waiting what the next exhibit would bring us, and if we would have gone to another subject, then I would have asked Mr. Harmon --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We are going to go through some additional exhibits, Your Honour, about whether Mr. Krajisnik was aware that there was ethnic cleansing taking place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So Mr. Stewart was a bit early in his --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Better to be cautious on the Defence side, Your Honour, and I accept, if we are, then the answer is yes. But I think we can be forgiven for being cautious in this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It would be easier to forgive you, Mr. Stewart, if it would be done a bit more efficiently, with less words, same content. Please proceed, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, just for purposes of this particular exhibit and asking the ensuing questions, can you tell me when we will be taking our break? Because this exhibit is 7 minutes and 56 seconds long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We had an early break. If we take a break now, that would -- I think we would have a break at approximately 12.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
