utterances.text: All right. That gives me guidance. Thank you very much. If we could play the exhibit. For Your Honours, the reporters, it is found at tab KID 31460. And before I play it, I want to give everyone time to find it in the respective binders.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I really would welcome guidance from the Trial Chamber on how on earth I could have made the point I made in less than the 16 seconds or so that I took. I hope I'm no too easily offended, Your Honour, but it is impossible for me to see how I could have made that point more efficiently. But if I'm wrong about that, and if there is some useful guidance the Trial Chamber could give me on how I could possibly have made that point more quickly, then I would welcome it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can we, Your Honour, address that after we finish --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we'll do that, not at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you. Okay. If we could proceed with this particular intercept, then. "Hello? Yes? Yes? Hello? Good evening. Good evening. Could I please speak with Mirko? Mirko? I'm calling from the cabinet of President Krajisnik. Oh, of course. Hold on, please, he'll be right here. Yes? Hello? Yes? Good evening, Mirko. Good evening. How are you? I'm all right, and you? Are you hanging in there? Some shooting's started. Really? Here, the president would like to talk to you. Hold on a moment, please. Put him on. Who is shooting? Hello? Hey, Milan. Hello. Hello. What's going on? What's new? Lots of things. You? My mate Momo is here, so I thought to ask you. Nothing. I don't know what would be worth doing. What's going on? I don't know what to tell you. Some shooting started just now. Where? Cannons around the village. Around the village? Yes. Well, what is it? Are you being shot at? We're just trying to find out. It's dark, you know. Did they inform you about that Karkin thing? Yes. We called the Presidency, but he had gone. I don't know even know where. 663-488. Yes. Milena called him. Stojko? Uh-uh. All right. Yeah, let me see... Does he know how to leave a message or... What did he tell you he wanted? Has Milan been to see you? Well, yes, but forget that. I know he only called me because I had called. This is -- he's called me from Izetbegovic's office to check. He asked you not to shoot the JAT skyscraper up there. His mother has been wounded and things like that. Not to shoot at the JAT skyscraper? Listen ... Vito called me. Yes? He's been up there today. Yes? So he wanted me to tell you the details and things like that. Has Simovic accepted this? Yes, but he says nothing will come of it. Why? He says the government is no good. He also told me there was a terrible fight in the Presidency session today. Why? He said it got really ugly. Alija wants either Pusina or that Gras, director of internal affairs. Yes? And the guy from Kladusa wants Delimustafic in that position, you know. Yes. So they offered Delimustafic's position in supplies or something like that. He said, Wait, Alija, I'm not here to work for you. I'm a rich man. I've supplied more goods in this war. You're obviously installing this Sandzak guy in the Gras. Then he said, It's easy for you to sit there in your easy chairs eating lamb while people up there... He told him all these things, you know. Did Simovic really accept this? Yeah. He accepted it? Yeah, but when this guy told him it was a shame he had done so, that it was a puppet government dominated by Muslims in which Serbs played a minor role, he said the government would fail because it wasn't set up properly. And Nikolic too, right? Did you see that? Ranko Nikolic? Well I can't believe he had the guts to do this. Well, they have done it. Their names are being published. Well, no, but I mean ... did they accept this or what? Well, I don't know. On the whole their names have been published. They wouldn't have published their names if they hadn't accepted. Yeah, that's just their proposal... Then this guy says today that things aren't really functioning in the Presidency. Kecmanovic said all kinds of things, you know. Yes? That people think the Serbs would get the Presidency, Alija can't get a third mandate. Yes. So, he says, you're thinking of becoming Presidency chairman, getting yourself a good deal, some position as an ambassador. Reportedly, the reformists have asked for Kecmanovic's removal. Why? Well, he's not following the party guidelines which put him in the Presidency. So they made the decision on Jure Pelivan without consensus, and all kinds of things. What about Jure Pelivan? The decision to appoint him Prime Minister. Oh, I see. No consensus was reached, you know. He said he had attacked Pejanovic. He gave me a telephone number in case you want to see... Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond Him? Yes. All right, give it to me. He has all kinds of things to tell. 619-494. What was that again? 619. Yes? 494. All right. He says hello. It wouldn't be bad if he were to call him, you know. Okay, but what is he doing there? He spent the whole day there after they had invited him. He was like, 'You will not drag me into these dirty affairs ... You ignore Serbs everywhere.' You'll hear all kinds of things from him. Call him up. All right. What's going on up there? Well, we've been really busy all day. Fuck, this morning I heard that the Muslims, who were running away from Misoca, killed a full busload of Serbs in Srednje. Misoca was being cleansed ... Yeah? So Muslims killed a full bus of Serbs ... How? ... who were on their way to Pale as refugees. Just a little while ago they told me this wasn't the case, but that, in fact, they took these prisoners with them. Actually, an older sergeant who does exchanges up there received a phone call from the city. Can you hear me? Say it again. This guy from the city called him, you know. But what was his name? Can't remember. Alispahic. And he said those prisoners had been killed. What prisoners? They took the prisoners to Pale again. Yes. At Srednje they were intercepted by Muslims who killed all those prisoners. Our two men have been heavily wounded. They thought those were our people? They thought those were our people. Yeah. Tonight they want to retaliate against all Serbs in the city and in prison. Yeah? To kill them all. Unbelievable. Supposedly, they will use their cutthroats to attack Rajlovac in groups and all kinds of things like that. That's what they called them. Unbelievable. To retaliate. All right. I'll talk to you later. Tell our people there I said hello. All right. Okay. Just, who sent that girl there? Well, she'll go tomorrow at 11.00. Go where? To Belgrade. Oh, really? Uh-huh. All right, then. Yeah. Well, these people haven't come, have they? Who? The two you talked about. Which ones? Oh, no. They will come. They will come. Today ... We'll do something about that tomorrow. We should do something about this thing down here. The insinuations are very possible. Fuck it. All right. I'll talk to you later. All right. Give it some thought. Check with the best man Momo about that, what he was supposed to do for Zarko, please. Yes. I've told him. All right. Call me before you go to bed. I'll be there. Yeah, we'll hang out a little longer and we'll ... I'll call you before I go to bed. All right. Have a good one. Bye. Bye."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, in this intercept of the 15th of June, 1992, Mirko Krajisnik tells Momcilo Krajisnik that Misoca, Muslims were running away from Misoca. Misoca was being cleansed. Do you know what kind of village ethnically the village of Misoca was?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do know. It is, in fact, a multi-ethnic village with a very small number of Croats and a vast majority of Muslims and a very negligible number of Serbs, perhaps 10 per cent or even less than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: My next exhibit is some demographic data, Your Honour, taken from the 1991 census, relating to the village of Misoca.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit number P299.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That exhibit, Your Honour, has the demographic distribution of the village of Misoca. Now if we could then turn to one other element in this particular intercept. I'd like to draw your attention to the following portion in the English translation. It's on page 3 of the intercept and it's where Mirko Krajisnik -- it's about a third of the way up. Mirko Krajisnik informs Momcilo Krajisnik: "He asked of you not to shoot at the JAT skyscraper up there."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, do you have some observations as to this particular part of the intercept?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, just in relation to this aspect, I would register the objection that of course a document speaks for itself, just as a telephone intercept speaks for itself. And if there are inferences to be drawn, they're for the Trial Chamber to draw, and a foundation has not been laid in relation to in which way the witness could possibly assist by giving an explanation of the conversation. This is a matter for the Trial Chamber to determine and not a matter for the witness to give evidence on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness could make observations in relation to a telephone conversation. For example, he could say it couldn't be -- he could say a JAT skyscraper does not exist, as far as I'm concerned. So therefore, it's totally not understandable what they're saying. And it's not something that the witness could nothing add to from his factual knowledge. So the objection is denied, Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, of course, we are in the luxurious position, of course, of having that particular outline, and I make my objection on the basis of what has already been foreshadowed might be forthcoming.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness may answer the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in respect of this particular sentence, "He asked of you" - he's referring to Momcilo Krajisnik - "not to shoot at the JAT skyscraper up there." Do you have some observations in respect of that particular request made to Mr. Krajisnik not to shoot at the JAT skyscraper?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't only linked to Mr. Krajisnik, but to other leading Serbs at Pale as well. And if you had any links to them or convection with them, you could help save your family, your house, or the place you were living in. So from the request made by this Sarajevo lawyer, it is obvious that the person in question had the power to do that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now we would like to play one additional intercept, Mr. Kljuic, and this is intercept from Exhibit 292. The KID number is 31469. This intercept lasts four minutes and 58 seconds, and I think I will have enough time to conclude my examination, assuming we proceed on schedule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Hello. Yes. Hello. Hi, hi. We've been waiting. Has he arrived? Just a minute. Yes. Yes. Hello, good morning, Momo, Milijana speaking. Hello, Milijana. How are you? Well... President Krajisnik wants to talk to you, just a moment. Hello. Yes. What's new, Mandic? Mr. President, how are things? I must tell you ... did you have the hiccups just now? I just said that you're a real hero. All the others are just useless. You're right in that one and for the rest we'll see. Useless, I must tell you. There are just a few Serbs with such name and that reminds me of Vojvoda Momcilo. Listen, Momo. Yes, tell me. Milos Savic's brother has been arrested. Right. And now listen to this ... Mr. President. Yes. The first part has been mopped up. It was done today. The first part has been mopped up. Yes, it's been mopped up. The first part has been mopped up. Which part? That one, the one that was uncertain. I don't know which one. Oh, the one up there? Yes. On the top, is it? Yes, yes. No kidding? Yes. Listen, and the men, they've already been transferred there. Is that right? Yes, they're working. Good, excellent. I have to tell you this for your ears only. This, I'm giving you compliments. Yes. Listen, please. Milos Savic has been arrested. Yes. Since you're in that commission, Savic Dusan. Okay. Savic Dusan, is that right? He's up there in that Knezevica potok, but his wife, sister-in-law, and his sister are there with him too. In which potok? You know, that is Knezevica potok. Where is that settlement? It's up there higher than Boljakov potok. Boljakov potok? Between Buca potok and Boljakov potok. Yes. Let me tell you... Savic Dusan has been arrested. Yes. But please, if you can, when you have time to contact them, you're in that commission, you know ... make a contact because his wife and all the others are going insane. Okay, okay, we'll put him for tomorrow. Done. What is that part? Yesterday when we were looking at that portion that was not clear ... Yes, okay, good. That has been done. And tell me, that stronghold, has it been put together? Yes, yes. I must tell you that you will be decorated, when the circumstances are right you'll get a medal... It's the people that did it. Yes. These specialists of mine. There are not many like that. No, okay, go ahead. Agreed Mr. President. I have seen this and you ... just a moment ... Milos is telling me something. Okay. Have a good time. Cheers. Momo. Yes. Please will you write down this house number. Yes. Okay. And what is the last name? Okay give me just the house number. Babic Dusan, 81 Dolacka Street. 81 Dolacka Street? Yes, he was captured yesterday on the 24th of June, 1992. 81. 81? Yes. When was he captured? Yesterday on the 24th of June about 7.00. Okay. Apparently the MUP men, some three cars, my house ... his house was searched, he was captured and so on. Okay. I kindly ask you ... Okay. Please do something. He's my brother... Okay. And is he for exchange ... Yes. I want to take everyone from there, my sister-in-law, brother-in-law and then let them set things on fire, loot and do whatever they want. Okay, okay, I'll put them on the list and we'll finish that. Here are the names of the others. Yes, give me their names. Savic Zorka. Savic Zorka. Savic Dunja. Savic Zorka, Dunja. Yes, Cucilo Nedeljko. Cucilo Nedeljko? No, yes, and Cucilo Slavojka, that's my sister. Cucilo Slavojka? Yes, there are also Dolacka Street, these two ... Dolacka number 83. Okay. Sorry 63. All 63, Dolacka Street? 63. The last two on the list, they're all on Dolacka Street. Okay. Please do something. We'll be in touch. Okay."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, can you, in respect of the portion of the intercept where there is a dialogue between Mr. Mandic and Mr. Krajisnik, the English translation reads: "President --" Krajisnik answers "Yes." This is found, Your Honour, on the second page of the English translation. "The first part has been cleaned. It's done today." Krajisnik: "Did it go?" Krajisnik -- I'm sorry. Mandic says: "Yes, cleaned up." Krajisnik: "Huh?" Mandic: "The first part has been cleaned." "Which part?" And Mandic answers: "That one, the one that was under question mark." Now, how do you interpret those words, Mr. Kljuic? You heard them.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mandic was the former deputy police minister and an operations man, and I think that in his government, in official terms, he had the status of minister of justice. And it is in fact a report according to which some part, certainly around the city of Sarajevo, had been cleaned, because regardless of their force, they were not able in the first stage to subjugate the whole surrounding parts of Sarajevo. There was sporadic resistance. And then it was thanks to the power they had, step by step, they cleared up the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This intercept, for the record, Your Honour, is -- I believe it is ten days after the previous intercept. This intercept, the one we have just heard, is dated the 25th of June, 1992. And that concludes my questions at the moment. I have some -- I will resume after the break, Your Honour, with some questions about intercepts as directed and instructed by Your Honour earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Harmon, I must admit that in the previous intercept, it went so quickly that where Serbians were killed in a bus and on the road to Pale, as far as I understand, as far as I understand, and in that relation, the word "cleansing" was used. It's not entirely clear to me what the position is. Perhaps you could clarify that after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes. I can clarify it now, Your Honour, if you'd like, or I can do it after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know whether -- if you want to give your interpretation of what happened, then it should be done not in the presence of the witness. So perhaps --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- we'll do that immediately after the break and see whether this clarifies at least the position of the Prosecution in respect of that exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll adjourn until 20 minutes past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm prepared to proceed, Your Honour. Before the witness comes in, I am prepared to proceed in the manner in which Your Honours have requested on these intercepts and I'm going to go through each of the intercepts in the binder and I'm going to direct the witness's attention to specific portions in those intercepts and ask him to comment on those. He had listened to those. It will require him to momentarily refresh his recollection on what the intercept is in its entirety. There is a separate issue that relates to this and I propose that the solution will be that I will lead him on this issue. In the chart that you have before you, there is a column where he has identified the speakers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And I propose to say: Did you identify in this intercept X and Y as the speakers, and I will be following as my guide the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could we do that in a bit different way? If we would have a copy of that document without any comments in it, just the speakers, and then go through that list. I mean, that might be easier. It's just copying the list once and then covering with a bit of white sheet of paper the comments and then we could go through that a bit more quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes. I could --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is exactly and precisely the suggestion that I made to Mr. Harmon about five minutes ago. So by definition I endorse it, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it, then, that of course it would be a bit of a surprise if he suddenly comes up and says, no, these are totally different persons. So perhaps we could do then that -- we don't have to do it immediately, I would say, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I can lay a foundation by asking him if in fact he had listened to the intercepts and had identified them and those identified speakers were reflected in the document that he signed and then I can redact the comments and submit those to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That would be -- let's solve that in the most practical way. Mr. Harmon, I asked you a question about the cleansing and the bus with the Serbs. That was -- because it was not entirely clear to me. That was about KID 31460.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes. I'm familiar with the passage that Your Honour is referring to and I can give you my interpretation of it, if that's what Your Honour requests.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At least it seemed that it was clear to everyone or not, but I didn't fully understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This -- intercept, Your Honour, this portion of the intercept is -- let me read it.: "Fuck, this morning I heard that the Muslims, who were running away from Misoca, killed a full load -- full bus of Serbs in Srednje. Misoca was being cleansed ..." What this intercept is saying is Mirko Krajisnik is informing Momcilo Krajisnik that the village of Misoca was being cleansed, that Muslims were running away from it, and as they were running away from it, they killed a full bus of Serbs in the village Srednje.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand from the transcript that the bus full of Serbs were refugees. Is that -- or were they prisoners? It's not --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Well, then it gets -- we have to -- beyond that we have to submit additional evidence. There's a discussion as to whether they were prisoners, as we go down below.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Alispahic and he said, Those prisoners had been killed. Mr. Krajisnik says: What prisoners? And then there's a discussion about the prisoners. And I think what, in my view, they are referring to people who were in the bus. That is a bit confusing, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But it is basically your understanding that Misoca was being cleansed means in this context that Misoca was cleansed by the Serbs although a busload of Serbs were on their way to Pale and then killed by Muslims who had fled that village.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, at least it's clear to me now what the Prosecution's position in this respect is. Whether it automatically follows and whether it logically follows from the text has to be considered, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Therefore, you're now aware that at least it raises some questions in the Chamber's mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I mention in relation to -- well, it's KID 31469.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's the Prosecution number, which I think should be the intercept considered immediately before the break. When Mr. Harmon puts the -- in fact follow-up questions, he read from the translation which referred to "cleaning." There appear to be two translations of this particular intercept into English, but the phrase which came across in the transcripts before Mr. Harmon's questions was "mopped up" or "mopping up," which is the phrase which appears in the translation -- well, the main translation, I'll put it that way, that we've been working from. There is really a difference, and I'm not quite -- we're simply not clear here about the status of these two rival translations. But it appears to us that "mopping up" is the correct translation rather than "cleaning."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But me not being a native speaker and knowing that none of my colleagues is, could you explain to me exactly what the difference then is between "mopping up" and "cleaning." Because I saw both terms used in similar context with, at first sight, similar meaning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. Let me start with something very simple. You can clean a floor in all sorts of ways, and that's general. If you are mopping up the floor, it generally implies that you're getting rid of bits of dirt and bits of problems on the floor. I think that's a fair summary. But applied to something less mundane, when we're talking about these things, "mopping up" is a -- and I'm confident this is correct: "Mopping up" is used in a military context, again in an analogous way, as a metaphor, that you are dealing with, for example, pockets of resistance. For example, if you've had a major operation in an area and it's been, say, largely successful, but you've got little pockets of enemy troops around, if you were to go in to eliminate them, those remaining pockets, that would be a "mopping up" operation, and that's how it's widely used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Removing the remaining particles.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. And one can see, as a metaphor, one can see exactly how that arises. Of course it matches cleaning in the sense that you've produced a clean result, in one sense, by that mopping up operation, but "mopping up" is the -- does have its own distinct connotation -- Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that the American --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- quasi-linguistic expert role.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't offer myself up as an expert in the B/C/S language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you immediately oppose it as saying this English interpretation of --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I think the word, from what I understand, can have two meanings, and I think it's up to the Court to attach the meaning it finds appropriate under the circumstances. That's why I asked --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course, the original language has to come first and that --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That is why I asked the witness what his impression -- he had listened to the intercept and what his impression of it was. In addition, Your Honours will be hearing evidence from the Sarajevo municipalities that may also augment and assist you in understanding this intercept.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, the very simplest way of dealing with it, I'd suggest --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's ask our interpreters first.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: May I make a practical suggestion, Your Honour: The very simplest way of dealing with it is simply to ensure that when, for example, Mr. Harmon uses the word "cleaning," or anybody uses the word "cleaning" or "mopping up," that's the word which is used in B/C/S is the word which appeared in the original transcript. Because if we have that, then there's no problem because the witness is getting what the original transcript in his own language, what the original conversation, the original speaker actually said, and then the English becomes irrelevant for those purposes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course it's not sure that the interpreters may always be in a position to immediately find -- perhaps if Ms. Cmeric could assist us and read the relevant line, which is, I would say -- let me just see where it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: It's on page 2, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I see it's just -- it seems to be the line which starts with the word "Onaj." Is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, just for the record, this translation that I have and that is in your binders is the official English translation from the CLSS services. So ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- we were given then, Your Honour. It's very confusing for us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please read that line, Ms. Cmeric, if you would be so kind, to assist us.

utterances.speaker: MS. CMERIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. [Interpretation] That first part was "cleansed" or "mopped up." Both translations are acceptable. "It was finished today."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note: We can only offer our opinion that the word "ciscenje" means cleaning, cleansing, and mopping up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It now becomes clear, Mr. Stewart, that the subtleties of the English and the difference between mopping up and cleaning or cleansing is not similarly existent in the B/C/S version. Then let's have --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes, I see. So is my suggestion going to be followed, then, that the witness is going to be given, in these questions, the original word that was used in the original conversation? Because that is the obvious, we submit obviously correct --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- way to proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But I also do understand that whether we, in English, say "cleaning," "cleansing" or "mopping up" it will be translated into the same word anyhow in B/C/S because no distinction is made.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: If that's right -- I'm sorry, if that's correct, then, yes, my practical suggestion is, by definition, adopted. That's all I want to be clear about. Because if there are two possible translations back into B/C/S, then we wish to make sure that the translation is the one that matches the original conversation. If there is only one translation back into B/C/S, then that happens automatically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's how I understand the observation by the interpreters. If I'm wrong, they'll certainly correct me. Madam Usher, could you please escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note: The word "mopping up" in English, this expression "mopping up" is usually translated into Serbian with a more precise term "ciscenje terena," meaning cleaning of the terrain or mopping up of the terrain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If the witness could be given the exhibit which, if I can find the number, it is 292, I believe, the binder of intercepts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, let me tell you how we're going to proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wonder if Your Honour does note the comment made by the interpreters, which is very pertinent to this particular point, and helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Certainly. If "mopping up" in English is used, then they'll use the same word in B/C/S but add the word "terrain" to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, that isn't what the interpreter said as we understand it. We're now interpreting what the interpreter said. The interpreter is saying that it's translated into Serbian with a more precise term. I understand that as meaning that there is a different word which may be used in Serbian. That's what seems to be saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's stop at this moment. Whenever we come to the word "cleaning," "cleansing," we'll see what to do. Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, let me tell you how we're going to proceed. You have in front of you a binder with intercepts. The binder has both English and B/C/S intercepts. Those intercepts are all intercepts that you have listened to, and you have had the opportunity to prepare a -- some comments in respect of each of those intercepts and you have identified the speakers in each of those intercepts. You've had a chance to review the list in the spreadsheets where you have, in respect of each intercept, indicated which speaker you can identify. And I take it you reaffirm that your identities of speakers in respect of the intercepts is accurate; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I am going to have to -- I will ask you questions in respect of each of these intercepts. I will not play these intercepts for you again in court, but I will ask you to follow my direction. I will give you the number in the binder with a specific intercept, and I would ask you to review the B/C/S translation of that intercept and then I am going to direct you to specific parts of the intercept and I'm going to ask you some questions about specific parts. But I want to give you the opportunity before I ask you those questions to please review the intercept in the language that you best understand. So if we could turn to -- and if the witness could be given, have the assistance of the usher as well so we make sure we're as efficient as possible, if you could turn to the first intercept, which is KID 30320. And this -- to double-check, this is an intercept of the 18th of July, 1991, and it is -- the B/C/S version is two pages. So if you could review that and tell me when you have finished reviewing that.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm ready now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, let me -- I will read to you the passages that I'm interested in and ask you to try to find them at the same time in the intercept. The passage I'm interested in first directing your attention to is found in page 2 of the English translation, in the middle of the page. And let me read you the passage and perhaps you can locate it. "Mr. Krajisnik: All right. I will go up there, then. Look here. In that thing. What's it's called? Han Pijesak. Oh, and listen another thing, please. Today, Radovan, we have to have -- we should have actually today and tomorrow a meeting with all our MUP cadres. I would organise it all. Karadzic: Aha. Krajisnik: But you should come as well. We have to clear things up with them and set an ultimatum, either withdraw all the men or not make a disgrace of ourselves with this. Karadzic: All right. Krajisnik: But do you want me to organise it? Just tell me when. Karadzic: You organise it. Organise it for, let's say, tonight at 6.00. Krajisnik: At 6.00? Karadzic: Yes. Krajisnik: All right. Then I'll organise it at 6.00." This is an intercept, Mr. Kljuic, that's dated the 18th of July, 1991. My first question to you is: Can you tell us -- strike that. Let me ask you, in terms of your previous testimony about the close collaboration between Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik, your views as to whether this intercept supports or does not support your position.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It clearly corroborates my opinion, because on a daily basis they agree on a plan of work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you mentioned that as well that there had been ultimatums. In terms of ultimatums in this intercept, can you offer the Court any comments?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is evident that the two of them held Serb policemen in joint, mixed institutions under their control very well. Namely, on every issue, be it a current, daily issue or a controversial one, all Serb policemen had to hold a similar view. That was particularly difficult to implement on the ground, because we wished for the Bosnia-Herzegovina police to be harmonious in terms of personnel, in view of the fact that at the time of the former Yugoslavia, the Serb policemen were represented in an excessively large measure in police force. This ultimatum Karadzic made to Sarajevo was part of his daily rhetoric, and in all disagreements, in all cases of disagreement, instead of discussing, in looking for a compromise, a compromise that is always indispensable in Bosnia and Herzegovina, he would always say we would withdraw from all the institutions, we will establish our own exclusively Serb institutions. And in this way, he was practically seeking to break up the constitutional system.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In this intercept -- a few lines below the passage I read, there's reference to somebody named Leovac. Can you identify who that person is?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In addition to the official SDS leadership, including the top leaders I've already mentioned, Karadzic set up a council which was supposed to include prominent Serb intellectuals. In fact, it included only those who supported the memorandum of the Serbian Academy of Science, and the most prominent among them were Milorad Ekmecic and Slavko Leovac. Slavko Leovac was chairman of that council, and generally speaking, both Leovac and Ekmecic were lecturers at the philosophy school of the Sarajevo university, whereas Ekmecic was also a member of the Academy of Sciences in Belgrade. They were expected to send a message on behalf of the intelligentia that what the SDS leadership was doing was right, they were supposed to lend it authority, and that anything else was contrary to the interests of Serbs in the territory of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, if we could turn to the next intercept in order. It is KID 30392. If you could familiarise yourself with the contents and then I will ask you questions about specific portions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, it would be most helpful if Mr. Harmon were able to give the date of each intercept as he introduces it, because we're working from a slightly different system here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The date of this intercept is the 26th of August, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, I take it that you have recently read through these intercepts. So therefore, if you feel that you can orient yourself without reading the whole text first, please indicate to Mr. Harmon when you are at a point where you -- it's in your recollection again what the intercept was about, and then he'll turn you to specific parts of that. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of these intercepts I have already read. I read them last year, preparing for testimony in the Milosevic trial. But I can answer questions without reading it all over again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please indicate when you feel comfortable that you are able to deal with any questions in relation to the intercepts. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you prepared to proceed on this particular intercept, Mr. Kljuic?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm ready.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me direct your attention to --

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- the first page. This is an intercept of the 26th of August, a conversation between Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik. And let me read the passage I'd like you to comment on. For Your Honours, it's on page 1, toward the top. This is Karadzic: "Mr. President, please tell me: Are you having problems with the women in the army?"

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: "Oh, fuck you. Fuck a hero who's with women. Where are you now?" Karadzic: "I'm at the clinic." Krajisnik: "I think we should adopt a very serious decision today. I think it's high time and the people are right in saying that." Karadzic: "Really." Krajisnik: "I think the parliament is finished. We should make it clearly known. Prepare people. It's over, Radovan." Karadzic: "Really." That's the passage I'd like you to comment on, please.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like, Your Honour, to describe briefly the context in which this was happening. The war in Croatia is raging full bore. In the territory of the whole Yugoslavia, mothers are demanding their children be returned from the army, one of the reasons being that the JNA had lost the confidence of the people, as well as its multi-ethnic purpose. The women in Sarajevo were also demanding their children back, the children that had been regularly mobilised, generation by generation. And when Karadzic asks Krajisnik, in derogatory terms, about the battalion of broads, it is a vulgar reference to the women's battalion, to these women asking for their children. On the other hand, we in the parliament were about to take a decision that soldiers from the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina could not be recruited for the war in Croatia, and since Croats and Muslims had already refused to go to battlefields in Croatia in their overwhelming majority, the only ones responding to call-ups were Serb volunteers. We're talking about here about boys who had already been in the army at the time when they were sent to the Croatian theatre of war. Since there was no goodwill for dialogue in the parliament and no goodwill to find a solution to protect all the children in Bosnia and Herzegovina, the BH parliament would become paralysed every now and then. In Karadzic's statement that this would come to nothing, this was going nowhere, and that it needed to be stopped, is not something that promises a solution in the future, and it's not geared to find a peaceful way of resolving it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the context of this particular passage, can you tell us whether the women who were opposed to the war did indeed visit the parliament?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A huge number of mothers resisted the participation of their children in that war, and a great number of them did indeed come to the parliament of Bosnia and Herzegovina, demanding to be received by the speaker. They demanded, in ultimatum terms, that their children be returned to them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me turn your attention to another passage. It's on page 2 of the English translation, a little bit below halfway down. Krajisnik: "The Croatian representative said today: Let me tell you, the HDZ held a press conference today. See here. Let's discuss this a bit and then we'll come over." Karadzic: "All right. Krajisnik: For a while. Tonight at 8.30. Karadzic: Yes. Krajisnik: Vojo and I will come over for a bit. Karadzic: "All right. At the press conference one of the journalists told me that he's crazy. He wants to leave the coalition to create a crisis. Well, let him create a crisis, the motherfucker. That's excellent. They wanted to push us to the margins of the political system several times so far. Now, that's excellent. Let him marginalise himself. That's excellent. Now intelligence will come to the fore. Krajisnik: All right. I'll come over and we'll come to an agreement." Can you tell me your assessment of that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this madman that Karadzic is referring to is myself. I was then president of the HDZ. It was me holding that press conference, where I said that we were not going to war against Croatia as part of the JNA, nor should our children continue to serve in the Yugoslav People's Army. And I explained why. I went on to say: If the current government does not support this position, we, as one of the three main parties in the coalition, would step out. How were we supposed to go on being part of that coalition if the people of that coalition were approving the aggression against Croatia and the killing of innocent people? And Karadzic then said that it was a good thing for them if I indeed took that step. Of course, I didn't make that step, because on that date we are discussing, I still believed that a compromise was possible in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Later on, Karadzic and his entourage would lose their nerve and walk out themselves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me turn to the next intercept, KID 30403 and the date on it is the 2nd of September, 1991. It is a conversation between Mr. Krajisnik and Mr. Karadzic. Can I proceed?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Yes, I remember the text.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let me direct your attention to the first part of the text and I will read the part I'm referring to. Krajisnik: "Hello." Karadzic: "Oh, hi." Krajisnik: "Hi, Doctor." Karadzic: "What's up?" Krajisnik: "Well I'm talking to some Serbs who could become good Serbs but haven't yet." Karadzic: "Oh, really." Krajisnik: "Can you imagine." Karadzic: "Is it Kecmanovic or isn't it? Krajisnik: "Ha, Kecmanovic, no. It's not Kecmanovic, by God. He's from a region with good households. You know what they're like. Kecmanovic is a city boy. You know he can never be a real Serb as this one is." Karadzic: "Yes, yes." Krajisnik: "Mr. Nedjo Miljanovic." Karadzic: "Ah, Nedjo Miljanovic." Krajisnik: "Yes, he says hello. Karadzic: "Well how much does he need? A lot or a little?" Krajisnik: "Let me tell you. He's short by a hair's breadth." Karadzic: "To be a good Serb." Krajisnik: "Well, that's the worst. That it's a hair's breadth. If it was more I would start working on him." Karadzic: "Uh huh. All right." Krajisnik: "Only a hair's breadth." Karadzic: "Say hello. Well, he should help us achieve the independence of that studio in Banja Luka, dammit." Krajisnik: "Well I can tell you from what he's doing now, I realise that you real Serbs are not even close to him." Karadzic: "Is he doing it wisely?" Krajisnik: "Well, wisely and superbly. He has some latecomer Serbs now. It's always a bit, you know." Okay. That's the passage I want to direct your attention to. Can you interpret that passage for us and can you identify who Mr. Kecmanovic is?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Kecmanovic was a university professor during communist times who, after Professor Koljevic left, came to the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina in a legitimate manner because he was third on the list on the Serb ticket in the elections. He was a member of the Presidency just briefly and then went to Belgrade via Pale. They did not consider him to be a good Serb, not because he was a city boy but because he did not become included in the SDS but was a member of the Reformist Party. And Kecmanovic did not join the SDS because he had personal ambitions of being the leader of the Bosnian Serbs, something he did not succeed in later on when he did actually go to Belgrade. Now, the second point that is important in this piece of dialogue is that in the offices of Mr. Krajisnik was the then director of the television of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Sarajevo. So the message that he should prepare the Banja Luka studio as best as possible meant that they should take as much as possible from joint property and relocate it to Banja Luka, so that, in future, the television would be in Banja Luka and that it would be powerful and up to the task in front of it. As far as I'm concerned, this was a shocking piece of information, namely, that the director of the joint television company was that close to the leaders of the SDS on such intimate terms. And today, from this distance of time, we can use that to explain the power that the SDS had in its propaganda machine via the illegitimate media, and that media in Bosnia was all important. And I, for example, as a leading politician in the country at the time - I was also president of a ruling party and thereby member of the Presidency - never had the possibility or was given the opportunity of explaining our political programme on television. All I could do on television was to take part in some joint programmes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me turn to another passage in the intercept. On the English version it's found on page 4, about a third of the way from the bottom. And this is the passage -- this is Karadzic speaking first: "Yes. Half an hour. Are you listening to that Grubac who is an SPO, Serbian renewal movement, adherent of the worst kind? They are the biggest traitors. They don't care about anything else. They don't care that the five-pointed star still exists, you know." Krajisnik: "Well, they are idiots." Then there's a break. "House on fire." And that's the passage I direct your attention to. Can you tell us -- Do you see the passage I'm referring to, Mr. Kljuic?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: First of all, can you tell us who Mr. Grubac is and why they're referring to him as the biggest traitor -- one of the biggest traitors?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Grubac was one of two representatives of the second ethnic Serbian party, the Serbian Defence Movement, the president of which is in Belgrade, Vuk Draskovic. They only had two representatives, and the SDS, 72, had 72. The SDS, therefore, considered that they had to blindly adhere to the directives of the SDS. And they didn't want to do that. But their motives were not that they wanted peace or a multi-ethnic Bosnia-Herzegovina. No. They did that for some separatist or separate goals. One of the things they wanted was to take the five-pointed star emblem away from the army caps that soldiers wore, for instance. And that is why these two men are saying that they're idiots and just out to secure their own interests.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me go to the next intercept. It's KID number 30406. This is dated the 4th of September, 1991, and it is a conversation between Mr. Krajisnik and Mr. Karadzic. Just cast your eye on that for a moment, Mr. Kljuic. Tell me when you're ready for me to proceed.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm ready.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. This -- I'm going to read you two passages, Mr. Kljuic. The first is found at the bottom of page 1 in the English and it refers to an incident that took place in the Serbian village of Kravica. I will read this. Karadzic: "Do you know that shots were fired up in --" Krajisnik: "I heard. Two dead, aren't there?" Karadzic: "Three. I think the third one is dead and two are seriously injured." Krajisnik: "All Muslims?" Karadzic: "All Muslims, but they attacked the Serbian village of Kravica." Krajisnik: "I'm not sure if that's true. You know what I said this morning. Please." Karadzic: "Yes." Krajisnik: "Cengic called me." Karadzic: "Really." Then I'm going to skip over a passage because I want to carry on on the top of page 2 in the English about five lines down. This is Krajisnik: "No, no. I also told Vito to make sure he goes up there and put in an appearance before the people. They are our people. You know, they become agitated. They want an army, they want all sorts of things, you know." Karadzic: "Yes. The army has set off from Tuzla." Krajisnik: "Yes. So that's -- oh, let them all just --" then there's a break -- "go to --" a break. "We must make sure that we put our point across today." Karadzic: "We'll make our point. You see, that's where it leads, where your policies lead." Krajisnik: "Exactly." Karadzic: "Can you see where this leads and do you realise that you will disappear in all of this?" Krajisnik: "Exactly." Karadzic: "Man, you will disappear. Many of us will also disappear, but you will be annihilated." Krajisnik: "No. We should say that we will all disappear, both sides, you know." Karadzic: "True." Krajisnik: "We should deliberately say this." Karadzic: "Exactly." Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond Krajisnik: "That's what should be done." Karadzic: "Yes." Krajisnik: "We should soften --" there's a break -- "toughen up. No." That's the end of the passage I'd like to ... First question: Can you very, very briefly tell us what happened, to your knowledge, in the village of Kravica, and then I want to turn my attention to the second passage.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This refers to an incident in which the Muslims had three dead and two seriously wounded and the accusation made was that they had in fact attacked that Serb village. In all similar situations, the Serbs asked the Yugoslav People's Army to step in, as being a guarantor of peace and security for them. But when the army actually did turn up, then they would have absolute power. Now, why Karadzic and Krajisnik didn't want Cengic to go, then he was the vice-president of the SDA at the time, was because any mixed commission could arrive at truthful information, could uncover the truth, and then could deduce who was to blame for that particular incident. And finally, yesterday we heard Karadzic's threats in parliament, in the BH parliament, made two months later. He never hid those threats, never masked his threats, when he said that unless such-and-such a thing were to happen, somebody would disappear. In this dialogue, in this conversation, we can see all the difference that exists between Krajisnik and Karadzic. Krajisnik, as the wiser of the two, says that it would have a better effect if we say all were to disappear, we will all disappear, as he says. But Karadzic had his own way of public speaking. He considered that he would raise his authority, lend more importance to himself, if he were to be the one to forecast the fate of individual ethnic groups in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And does this intercept again reflect the close working relationship between Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we can turn to the next intercept.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This intercept, Your Honour, I will -- the next intercept is KID 30656, and I will only -- I will not be asking Mr. Kljuic any particular questions about this. There has been sufficient foundation for name recognition in this. And we can then pass -- no, I'm sorry. Let me look at my next -- yes. If we could turn then to the next intercept that I'd like to ask some questions about. It is KID 30821.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's of the 6th of December, 1991?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That is the 6th of December, 1991. If you would take a look at that, Mr. Kljuic. Do you have the intercept of the 6th of December, 1991 before you?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is a rather long intercept, but I'm going to be asking you about, on the English translation, a passage that is found starting on page 2 of the English translation and going over to the top of page 3. Are you ready to proceed, Mr. Kljuic?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me read the passage. I'm referring to, on the English translation, it is found, well, at the top of page 2, and it reads as follows: Karadzic: "Well, he first let me say what I thought. I said that was out of the question, that we thought that needed not be, that this was a very sensitive balance, very frail balance, which we have managed to maintain. We have maintained it. And that the arrival of any foreign military force in Bosnia and Herzegovina, which is a part of Yugoslavia, would disrupt the balance. And then those two, they have positioned themselves divinely." Krajisnik: "Yeah." Karadzic: "They started bad mouthing Serbia. They started to -- they said they needed the military observers and the foreign forces here because Bosnia was cramped with army and could be neutralised with the United Nations forces only and that they would never let Bosnia stay in Yugoslavia." Krajisnik: "Both of them?" Karadzic: "Yes. Yes, and things like that, you know. And then when I -- second round now. I have a right to talk again, and I say: I am grateful to Mr. Mahmutcehajic and Mr. Kljujic." Krajisnik: "The two of them were present?" Karadzic: "Yes, yes. They told Mr. Mahmutcehajic and Mr. Kljujic what they needed for the United Nations forces for. That is the thing I have already told you about in Belgrade. They want the United Nations forces to confront the Yugoslav People's Army and neutralise it, with the help of the United Nations. They want to use the United Nations to solve --" Krajisnik: "Yeah." Karadzic: "To solve the political crisis. Yes, they want to use their presence to effect the solving of the political crisis. In one word, all our -- all our doubts and fears have come true and now you can see why the Serb side can't accept that. I screwed them badly. Then Marek Goulding said: Gentlemen, you have unfounded great expectations from the United Nations' presence, and your minister, Karadzic, have unfounded great fears because the United Nations will not do what has just been said. They would be here in the presence of unarmed observers, but only if you all agree, and so on, you know. I said we couldn't agree, because that might trigger a civil war, an inter-ethnic and interreligious conflicts, and that the United Nations bore a huge responsibility, that this was Yugoslavia, and the Yugoslav army maintained the public order here along with the Ministry of the Interior, and so on, you know. I simply screwed them. They have -- then that one bad mouthed Serbia and so on. Kljujic." Krajisnik says: "Yeah." That's the passage I'd like you to discuss. This is an intercept of December 6th, 1991.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I speak, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You may answer the question.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that time, the war operations in Croatia were drawing to a close. The status quo remained. 40 per cent of the territory was won over by the Serb rebels. And in Sarajevo, 20 days later, after this conversation, we would have a peace signed, a provisional peace of three years. The whole of the Yugoslav army that was withdrawn from Slovenia and Croatia, all the troops were brought to Bosnia. Then the reserve corps also came in from Montenegro and Serbia. The paramilitary formations and volunteers arrived. So with a set-up of this kind, Bosnia was in actual fact occupied, and it was not possible to conduct normal political negotiations with the SDS. The only thing that we could do and request was to have the UN forces come in first, as a preventive measure, and since the UN forces would only arrive if there was a consensus, and there was no consensus because Karadzic and his men did not want to accept the UN force's arrival. That was the first point. And second, we asked for observers, monitors. So that means unarmed observers coming from the United Nations. Because we believed that once those people arrived and saw the situation in the field, that they would be able to clearly inform the United Nations about our position. However, Karadzic did not accept any of these things, apart from having the Yugoslav army come in. For us Croats and for the vast majority of Muslims, that army had been completely compromised. You must know that before that, it had committed crimes in Dubrovnik and Vukovar and other parts of Croatia, and the people had a revulsion towards that army, the army which had lost the Yugoslav character and sense that it once had under Josip Broz Tito, and that was that it was a popular national multi-ethnic army. So the army then was exclusively composed of the leading cadres of Serbs and Montenegrins afterwards. And as an example of this, on the 24th of December of that same year in the BH Presidency we had a top-ranking delegation from the JNA, led by the defence minister of the day, Mr. Veljko Kadijevic. It was a top-level delegation. It had 14 leading generals. There was just one Slovenian admiral, Admiral Brovet. But apart from that, there was not a single Croat or Muslim among the delegation. I asked Kadijevic on the occasion: How do you think that the Croats - because I was the leader of the Croats - how do you think the Croats will accept that army, when you have failed during the negotiations to have one leading Croat officer in the JNA? His brutal answer was that everybody will listen to what the army says. So our efforts for a peaceful solution to the crisis was that we should have the UN forces come in, or at least UN observers and monitors, and the answer that was given you have heard through the intercept and conversation mentioned earlier on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I direct your attention, then, to an intercept that is one, two, three tabs later. It should be KID ID 30911. This is an intercept of 1 January 1992, a conversation between Mr. Krajisnik and Mr. Karadzic. It starts out with the words: "Hey, what's up?" I'm not quite sure the next word is exactly a literal translation, but ... 30911. Take a look at that, if you would, Mr. Kljuic, and then I'm going to direct you to a passage that's toward the end of that intercept.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And Your Honours, the passages that I'm going to direct Your Honours' attention to start on page 5. There will be a second passage on page 6. I can read the passage to you, Mr. Kljuic. It's a passage that deals with releasing tigers. So if you could find that particular part, then I will read it into the record.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm ready, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me read, then, the passage that starts on the English translation the top of page -- the third line down from page -- from the top of page 5. Radovan Karadzic: "He was like, 'If we're all the same, this and that, in a sovereign and independent Bosnia.' Now he's talking openly of a sovereign and independent Bosnia. Does he want to destroy Sarajevo?" Krajisnik: "Yeah." Karadzic: "Fuck. He's really crazy. Now he openly talks of a sovereign and independent Bosnia." Krajisnik: "Yeah." Karadzic: "You know that --" Krajisnik: Yeah. Karadzic: It was until recently fuck him we will release our tigers and let them do their job. Krajisnik: "Yeah. Can you imagine this impertinence?" Karadzic: "Fuck. I've -- we've been calming the Serb people for a year because of his foolishness. What can I do? I will not be calming anyone any more, nor can I." Krajisnik: "No, but he says we don't want -- this isn't an independent -- that's not a state, he says, it's a sovereign. So it is equal in the talks. Now he says independent. Fuck him. They really are crazy. Europe is crazy too if they think this can be so. Man, this is impossible. This -- I don't think there's a man who could turn the situation around now and make it so." Karadzic: "Na, Na." Krajisnik: "Na. Those are --" and there's an unknown term -- "man." Karadzic: "No way. We need to release those people. We shouldn't hold them back." Krajisnik: "We have to, but they'll do it anyway whether you want them to or not." Karadzic: "Like I said, you can't hold them back any more." Krajisnik: "No way. And what does this mean now? 'I really appreciate you Yugoslavs as a nation,' I said. Now, they too have some crazy ideas, but I said this softly. They want me to help them in the parliament so they can get the status of constitutive people." Karadzic: "Yeah." I will not read any further in that particular passage. Can I have your comments as to that particular passage. Go ahead, Mr. Kljuic.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As the situation became increasingly difficult for the citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina, especially for the non-Serbs, because of the constant increase of military materiel and equipment and pressure being exerted via the media at the same time and incidents breaking out in the field, and based on everything we had seen that had happened in Croatia, as well as the witnesses and young men who left the Yugoslav People's Army during that time and the behaviour of the SDS leadership, bearing all this in mind, there was less and less chance that Bosnia-Herzegovina, as a state itself, would remain connected to Milosevic in Belgrade in any way, that it would have any more ties, anything more to do with them. So I claim and state that at the beginning, the idea wasn't to separate Bosnia from Yugoslavia, but that through their violent actions and the force they used and the way in which they misused the army, they did everything to give us Hobson's choice and not have us enter into any kind of ties with Belgrade. And that is why our requests went along the lines of having Bosnia-Herzegovina from the very beginning on a footing of equality, just like all the other republics of the former Yugoslavia, that it have an equal footing. But ultimately, this led to the demand for independence, just as Slovenia and Croatia had done before that. For us to gain popular support for this idea, we organised a referendum, under very difficult conditions, but as you know very well, over 64 per cent of the electorate went out to vote in favour of an independent Bosnia-Herzegovina. So the conclusion that we can make on the basis of this conversation between Karadzic and Krajisnik is that they were not interested in any kind of equality in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in respect of the sentence by Mr. Karadzic, "We'll release our tigers and let them do their job," how do you interpret that?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the traditional method of coercion they were using, because they were in possession of armed forces, whether they belonged to the Yugoslav People's Army, the paramilitary units outside of Bosnia and Herzegovina, or autonomous forces within Bosnia and Herzegovina. In some sort of nationalist euphoria, they were looking to solve the national issue in Bosnia and Herzegovina by force, and their demands did not imply any dialogue or discussion. On the contrary; thanks to the advantage they had in terms of armaments, they thought they would be able to deal with it fairly quickly. This allusion to the wolves that were on standby was one of Karadzic's key arguments in every discussion. He would say: How long do you think we would go on discussing this? How long do you think I can keep the wolves on leash? They would like to come in and deal with things themselves. So it was not Karadzic's intention to go on with political discussions. He was using threats to make ultimatums. I never even thought, it never crossed my mind, that I could accept such ultimatums, particularly in view of the fact that the Croatian people in Yugoslavia had suffered great sacrifices even before the aggression. But the events of 1991 showed us best what was in store for us if those tigers from Bosnia were indeed released.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me turn to one other passage in this particular intercept. It's found on the English translation at the bottom of page 6. And let me read this to you, Mr. Kljuic. Krajisnik: "We have to use the first opportunity to tell him that he's playing with fire and we'll say clearly that they're playing with fire." Karadzic: "We will not tell him in private, but we shall do so in public, and him --" Krajisnik: "Yeah, in public. That's what I meant." Karadzic: "In private we'll tell him some other things." Krajisnik: "Yes, yes, that's all clear. Fuck. All right." Okay. That's the end of the passage I'd like to read. Can you comment as to that particular passage, Mr. Kljuic? Do you see it, and can you comment on it?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the later developments, we started preparing for independence. It was not just a military aggression that took place in Bosnia. Huge amounts of money were being printed in Belgrade, and at the time, it was in fashion to trade using foreign currency. Special units of people, smugglers, received money from Belgrade to buy German marks from the citizenry. The Yugoslav dinar had already been put out of circulation in Croatia, in Slovenia even before that, and now we were wishing Bosnia-Herzegovina to get its own currency too. That was another occasion for Karadzic to repeat his threats. He possibly -- maybe he thought that we were supposed to use the Belgrade currency forever, the currency that they were going to print and we were going to use.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does this passage reflect the close collaboration between Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. I regret very much that I now heard Mr. Krajisnik speaking in even more vulgar terms than Karadzic, who was very vulgar in his speech.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we can turn to the next intercept. I'll direct your attention to, Your Honour. It is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, before you do so, may I just for the record note that when you move to the next paragraphs on the last intercept, you also moved from KID 30911 to KID 30985.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes. I did that intentionally, Your Honour, because I know my time is limited and I can only --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But otherwise people might -- we even had some problems in finding page 6, where it seems to end at page 5. But we now move to the next one. That would be --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The next one -- it should be two tabs beyond. It's KID number 31023 [Realtime transcript read in error "21023"].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: It says January 1992. It is a conversation between Mr. Krajisnik and Mr. Karadzic. I'll wait, Mr. Stewart, for your signal to tell me you've found it, and then I will ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm sorry. It's just without -- it just says January, does it? Can you just give me the first words, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: It says: "What are you doing, Doctor?"

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I don't want to hold things up. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you see the intercept, Mr. Kljuic? And please, the passage I'm going -- if you would read the first -- or review the whole intercept.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: There appears to be an error in the transcript or I misspoke, it says 21023. The intercept is 31023. So if the record could stand corrected.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kljuic, give me your signal when you're finished, I'll proceed. The passage I'd like to direct your attention to appears, at least in the English on page 2, about a third of the way down. It read as follows: Krajisnik: "Down from municipality. Novo Sarajevo -- Novi Sarajevo, Novo Sarajevo." Karadzic: "Yes." Krajisnik: "It has to do with Birac. Me and you and him and the two of them sit down. They say there are small problems down there, and that is an important municipality for us." Karadzic: "Yes. Of course. And Birac I think that he is anyway very intelligent, has a good presentation, but does not catch." Can you comment on that small passage that I read to you.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN KLJUIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That seems to indicate that Krajisnik and Karadzic had insight into everything that was going on on the ground. And if you look at the date, the issue of Nova Sarajevo was very important because in that area near Pofalici, the city is at its narrowest, only a couple of hundred metres. And on one of the sides of this area is one of the largest barracks in Bosnia and Herzegovina, holding a great number of soldiers. In the eyes of the SDS, Nova Sarajevo was very important, because in their plans to cut the city in two, this point between Miljacka river and Pofalici was crucial. The distance is only 200 to 300 metres between these two points. Later, after this conversation, on two or three occasions, barricades would be put up in the city, fanning the tensions and anxieties among the citizenry, which is an overture to the upcoming aggression and a sort of rehearsal to see whether Sarajevo could be cut in two near Pofalici. The citizens of Sarajevo were also aware of the importance of this point in town, and defence had been prepared. So that in spite of all the preparations, they did not manage to cut the city in half, because the old town, where the parliament, the Presidency, and other government agencies were, would have been cut off had they succeeded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kljuic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I see the time, Your Honour, and I think it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Usher, would you escort Mr. Kljuic out of the courtroom after I have asked him to return to this same courtroom, Madam Registrar, tomorrow morning at 9.00, and after having instructed you, Mr. Kljuic, not to speak with anyone about your testimony, whether given or still to be given. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, how much time would you think you'd still need for the examination-in-chief? Of course, I'm aware that we had a lot of technical problems, that Mr. Kljuic may have arrived late, and therefore his comments were put on paper in a rather late stage. I'm aware of the problems, but nevertheless you said several times that Mr. Kljuic had to return Thursday.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I think it's unrealistic, frankly, to expect Mr. Kljuic to not -- he has to come back, I think, and I think there's no question that if he finishes -- and I can't talk to him, so I can't discuss with him his schedule. THE COURT: That's the reason why I raised the issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I will probably have an hour, I think. I'm going through these intercepts, I've made some selections. I think I can finish in approximately an hour or a little bit longer than that. It depends how many more of these intercepts --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you say -- if we have got another hour, well, that means, well, let's say in general terms, two days, which makes eight hours, nine hours, under normal circumstances, and I'm also looking at the Defence, 60 per cent of nine hours, would it be approximately close to six hours. But I can imagine that with this witness that the normal balance would not be adhered to by the Defence. Of course, we would have to discuss that. But if you say Mr. Kljuic has to return Thursday, would that mean that he is not available on Thursday any more or that he would leave, let's say, later in the afternoon on Thursday?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the problem is I am not able to talk to him about his schedule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You indicated several times Thursday. I thought you might have -- okay. We'll ask the Victims and Witness Unit to find out whether he's still available on Thursday in the morning, or what his schedule is. And then, Mr. Stewart, do you have any idea two issues: The first, whether you'd be able to start the cross-examination; and the second one, how much time it would take.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can certainly start the cross-examination. So far as the time is concerned, I would aim to be around the normal guideline. But it's early for that, Your Honour. Can I just make one specific request, though, Your Honour? I wonder if I could be told now, this afternoon, whether Mr. Kljuic is going to continue on Thursday or go home. It does significantly affect planning. So if I could know that straight away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's the first thing on our agenda, that we'll check with the Victims and Witness Unit at what time Mr. Kljuic is unavailable to us on Thursday, whether it would be for the whole day or only later on on that day and then we'll inform you as soon as possible. Because if he's not available Thursday during the morning, we'll certainly not finish the whole of his examination, because I take it that you would not be able to do it in three hours, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: There's no chance of that, Your Honour, and it would make a significant difference to the most useful use of time if I were to know straight away. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll find out as soon as possible. We'll inform you as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, could the Witness Unit also inform Mr. Kljuic that if he does leave on Thursday, in all likelihood he will be required to come back so he can measure whether he can make changes in his plans and stay this week for the remainder of the week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. To find the best solution also for himself, you would say. That's the first thing on our programme, to contact the Victims and Witness Unit and inform the parties as soon as possible. We'll then adjourn until 9.00 tomorrow morning, same courtroom.
